#6671. Steven Spielberg Believes Empathy Is Our ‘Only Real Superpower’

The veteran filmmaker was honored at the 18th annual MoMA Film Benefit with Chanel.

As rain poured down on Manhattan Thursday night, so did the tributes to Steven Spielberg. The veteran director was honored at this year’s MoMA Film Benefit, presented by Chanel, with homages from fellow icons of cinema and collaborators including Martin Scorsese, Tom Cruise, Emily Blunt, and Ariana DeBose. To top off the night, Spielberg (and the crowd) was treated to a surprise acoustic performance by Bruce Springsteen.

Honoring Spielberg’s contributions to film feels like a no-brainer, given the dozens of masterpieces he has delivered in his decades-long career, spanning Jaws, E.T., the Indiana Jones franchise, Schindler’s List, Jurassic Park, Saving Private Ryan, and many more, all the way up to Disclosure Day, which was just released this summer. Reflecting on his latest, Spielberg said in his speech, “It’s less about aliens and more about empathy. Empathy is the only real superpower that humanity possesses. It’s the only form of magic, I think, that exists in the world.”

And while he accepted the honor solo, the director said he shares the recognition with the hundreds of people in his casts and crews, including those who work at craft services. He also took a moment to thank his wife.

“When you honor me, you are also honoring my wife, Kate Capshaw, because the stuff I put in each of my films is from the stuff of life, real life, that Kate and I have created with family, friends, and conversation, and being aware that there’s more to living than just what we do for a living,” he said. “The confidence she’s given me every day for the past 43 years, I would not be the same person, or the same filmmaker, without her central to my very human existence.”

The program included opening remarks from Cruise, who starred in Minority Report and War of the Worlds, followed by a speech from Scorsese, who reflected on his decades of friendship with Spielberg. “Listen, we’ve known each other since 1972—how did we get to be in our eighties? What happened?” he joked. DeBose, who starred in Spielberg’s West Side Story remake and won an Oscar, performed “Somewhere” from the legendary musical.

Blunt, who starred in Disclosure Day, revealed that the back of Spielberg’s director’s chair is labeled with “Dad.” “‘Dad’ still has this childlike enthusiasm, this spontaneity,” she said. And when he’s “happy with a take, you’ll see him, he’ll just come running out of the tent with his fists in the air, and he’s cheering, and it’s like the best damn moment of your career,” she added. Spielberg later returned the praise, saying Blunt “could play any role—including James Bond.”

Steve Martin and Martin Short alternated zippy one-liners while introducing the guest of honor (they even joked about how many awards they shared between the three of them). And Stephen Colbert helped introduce the grand finale, Bruce Springsteen, who sang “Dancing in the Dark” on his guitar. Before jumping into song, The Boss took a moment to say a few words about Spielberg too, recalling the summer when Jaws first came out when he was living on the Jersey Shore. There used to be a tradition called night swimming, where people would swim in the ocean nude, often with someone they were interested in. But ever since Jaws, “Steven Spielberg fucked that up. He fucked it up good,” Springsteen said, to a room of laughter.

Other attendees included Drew Barrymore, Cate Blanchett, Robert De Niro, Jeff Goldblum, Riley Keough, John Krasinski, Donna Langley, Spike Lee, Lorne Michaels, Michelle Pfeiffer, Zoe Saldaña, Francesca Scorsese, Christopher Walken, and Michelle Williams. Jennifer Lawrence and Cooke Maroney made a low-key appearance.

#6669. Florence Pugh Sees Your Statement Coat and Raises You a Statement Shoulder

Forget the statement coat. Florence Pugh is all-in on the statement shoulder. And, in true Florence Pugh fashion, she’s doing nothing by halves. At an East of Eden FYC event in Los Angeles, the actor arrived wearing a black satin Harris Reed ensemble with shoulders of such exaggerated proportions that they practically deserved their own invitation.

Styled by Rebecca Corbin-Murray, Pugh wore a look from Reed’s spring 2027 collection, featuring enormous, sculptural sleeves that rose above her head like a pair of black wings. Beneath all that architectural drama was a tightly fitted, button-front corseted jacket and a slim pencil skirt, a silhouette that balanced Victorian severity with something subversive. (The look actually first appeared in the bridal-focused collection in all-white, but Pugh and Reed decided on the more gothic vibe.) She added towering Vivienne Westwood platform sandals and a constellation of diamond earrings from Maria Tash.

It’s hardly surprising that Pugh would turn to Harris Reed for such a theatrical yet elegant moment. The British designer is a longtime friend and collaborator: Pugh opened his fall 2023 London Fashion Week show in a sequined harlequin gown and enormous halo headpiece, delivering a Shakespeare-inspired monologue about the transformative power of clothes. She returned to open his fall 2025 presentation at Tate Britain, emerging in a pointed black corset and hooded gown for an eerie, dramatic performance. Reed’s designs, with such unabashed romanticism and allegiance to craft, have long been a natural extension of Pugh’s own fashion sensibilities.

The beauty look was equally striking. Makeup artist Alex Babsky gave Pugh a deep, wine-stained lip, softly smoked mauve-gray eyes, and flushed cheeks, while hairstylist Adir Abergel twisted her blonde hair into a deliberately undone, almost Regency-style updo, with wisps escaping around her face.

The night before, Pugh had embraced a more relaxed take on historical dressing. She appeared alongside her East of Eden co-star Zoe Kazan in a richly patterned Ralph Lauren Collection jacquard Maurice jacket, layered over the matching Thurlow corset top and a dark, floor-length Janie maxi skirt. She added Bulgari Serpenti Viper jewelry, Maria Tash diamond earrings, and chunky Christian Louboutin platform sandals to keep things modern.

Throughout the East of Eden promotional circuit, Pugh and Corbin-Murray have found a particularly satisfying meeting point between the actor’s maximalist instincts and the romantic, historical world of the Netflix adaptation. There have been enormous black Rodarte ruffles, a corseted Vivienne Westwood gown in shocking chartreuse, and an Erdem ensemble that paired sparkling lingerie with a kilt—the prettiest looks always come with a rebellious streak. While this time the finishing touch was the XXL shoulders, she recently made her red carpet debut with boyfriend Finn Cole on her arm.

Corsetry has emerged as a common thread, but Florence Pugh has never been one to play the demure period heroine. The bigger the shoulders, the better.

#6666. E.T., Phone Chanel! How Fashion’s Labels Got Personal Again

E.T., phone home! Or if you’re Steven Spielberg getting honored at the Museum of Modern Art’s annual Film Benefit, phone Chanel. On Thursday night, Spielberg offered a peek inside his bespoke Chanel tuxedo jacket, courtesy of Matthieu Blazy. Beneath the classic black tailoring was a galaxy-speckled lining, an embroidered playing card featuring E.T. on his bicycle, and a little patch reading “E.T. PHONE HOME.” Spielberg proudly flashed the details for all to see. Now that’s a statement lining.

It’s just the latest in a series of delightfully personal flourishes coming out of Blazy’s Chanel atelier. For his spring 2026 haute couture debut, the designer asked models to contribute something meaningful to their looks: a love letter, a birth date, a lucky symbol, an intimate thought. These were translated into exquisite embroideries by the house’s Lesage atelier, stitched into garments or onto little silk notes tucked inside delicate, translucent Chanel handbags. Model Stephanie Cavalli reportedly chose a letter from her husband. The sentiment was just as beautiful as the craftsmanship.

Blazy has continued to play with this notion of garments carrying memories. In the lead up to the spring 2027 Chanel show, models Bhavitha Mandava and Awar Odhiang discovered embroidered playing cards tucked inside jacket linings, depicting Gabrielle Chanel wearing looks the models themselves had previously walked down the runway in.

Couture clients can reportedly request this kind of personalization, too. And at October’s Academy Museum Gala, meanwhile, Hailey Bieber’s custom bubblegum-pink Chanel gown concealed another tender, handwritten detail: a note that featured the name of her son, Jack, accompanied by an arrow-pierced heart.

Leaving something deeply personal inside a garment is hardly new. Alexander McQueen famously made a rebellious art of it. While working for Romeo Gigli in Milan, the young designer reportedly left a rather less romantic message inside a jacket after being made to repeatedly redo its construction: “Fuck you, Romeo.” There are also the legendary tales—though disputed—of profanities hidden inside suits made for Prince Charles during his Savile Row apprenticeship. More poignantly, McQueen stitched locks of his own hair into the linings of his 1992 graduate collection, Jack the Ripper Stalks His Victims, and later used them in his clothing labels.

But the clothing label itself has also long been a place for designers to express a little personality. Spend an afternoon rifling through the racks of any good thrift store and you’ll find a rag-tag assortment of embroidered crests, elaborate cursive fonts, wacky illustrations, and wonderfully earnest mottos from long-forgotten local dressmakers to grand houses. Even Burberry’s evolving labels offer a miniature history of the brand: from the old Burberrys name and the original Equestrian Knight emblem, introduced in 1901, to the pared-back modernist identity of recent years, and Daniel Lee’s revival of the knight in 2023. A label can do so, so much more than simply announce who made something.

A new generation of designers is rediscovering the joy of these small, characterful details. Take Sofia Testino, whose young eponymous label imagines a whole world of professions and their fictional, more off-kilter wardrobes. It’s been a joy to watch her brand identity develop through old-fashioned woven labels, with evolving colorful geometric borders, winged crests, and the tagline: “Style, Quality, Value.” There are shoeboxes bearing a cartoonish evolution from ape to woman in high heels. Testino has spoken about collecting vintage labels and old flight-attendant uniforms, mixing and matching elements to create her own distinctive identity. “I feel like labels and packaging and all these little details have been lost,” she recently told Welcome.jpeg. Where so many brands have settled for homogenizing, identity-flattening minimalism, she’s building an entire universe (and its fleet of well-dressed staff) down to the last stitch.

Elsewhere, London-based knitwear designer Oscar Ouyang has made a sweet little lamb a recurring signature, appearing on his whimsical knits and charming clothing labels. For her recent collaboration with Frankies Bikinis, Devon Lee Carlson joined forces with longtime friend Francesca Aiello to revisit treasured vintage pieces from their own wardrobes, complete with sweet pink co-branded labels decorated with a little dog and flowers. And in another corner of London, Sinéad O’Dwyer has been rethinking her brand identity as her customers grow up alongside her, with her newly imagined logo finding its way into the stitching on the back of her jeans.

For London-based demi-couture designer Ellie Misner, a clothing label can also serve as a little love letter commemorating a particularly special moment. Misner, who works on bespoke pieces, has taken to hand-embroidering her clients’s names above her own handwritten logo. For Raye, who fulfilled a long-held dream by headlining Reading and Leeds Festival, Misner stitched her name in burgundy thread into a crimson corseted gown. For Tems, whose Glastonbury main-stage performance marked another career milestone, it was a cobalt-blue signature sewn onto the inside of a midnight-blue ensemble. “My labels are my handwriting,” Misner tells Vogue, explaining that she handwrites the wearer’s name and then embroiders it, often choosing a thread that corresponds with the garment. For a performance that means so much to both artist and designer, it’s a way of marking the occasion, making the piece feel like more than just another custom commission. Misner likens the gesture to “a love note to their garment.” She adds: “I wish I could do it for everyone,” but the time-consuming process makes each one all the more special. These aren’t all bespoke gestures in the couture sense, but they share a certain spirit that insists on individuality, as well as the pleasure of details that one can keep entirely to oneself.

There’s something especially resonant about all this in an age of AI-generated images, algorithmically dictated taste, and increasingly impersonal consumption. Fashion, more and more, seems keen to remind us that there are actual people, with skills and emotions behind the clothes. At Chanel’s fall 2026 couture show, artist Joël Blanc painted the runway live in watercolors, capturing the spectacle in real time. And look at the new holiday campaigns from Prada, Dior, and Bottega Veneta, where all three have embraced the nostalgic charms of illustration and animation. Prada, in particular, has made a point of celebrating hand-drawn artistry, enlisting veteran animator John Pomeroy to conjure a whimsical winter wonderland populated by snow lynxes and mischievous mice.

In a world where almost anything can be reproduced, the idiosyncratic and intimate feel increasingly precious. The most meaningful thing about what we wear might be something nobody else can see.

#6664. ELLE Escapes: Río Grande

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Puerto Rico has long been one of my favorite island destinations for a little rest and relaxation. Time and again, I find myself drawn back to the charming towns dotted along its northern and northeastern coasts. This month, my travels brought me to Río Grande, a tranquil, picturesque municipality affectionately known as La Ciudad de El Yunque (The City of El Yunque).

Just a 30-minute drive from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport, Río Grande offers a calmer setting than the bustling streets of San Juan, while still keeping the capital city’s attractions within easy reach. Beloved for its lush landscapes, breathtaking scenery, and abundant flora and fauna, the area is also home to a significant portion of El Yunque National Forest, which, fun fact, is the only tropical rainforest in the U.S. National Forest System.

Whether you prefer lounging poolside with a piña colada, venturing into the rainforest for a scenic hike, or heading west to meander through the vibrant streets of Old San Juan, I’ve found that Río Grande makes for an idyllic home base to experience the best of what the island has to offer.

Ahead, discover my recommendations for where to stay, what to eat, and what to explore in this enchanting corner of Puerto Rico.

Taking a nature walk or scenic hike through El Yunque National Forest is a must when visiting Río Grande. Whether you book a guided tour or venture out on your own with a rental car, there are trails suited to every experience level. Along the way, you’ll be stunned by the sheer variety of plants and wildlife you encounter. On my trip, I finally put a face to the symphony of chirps I’d been hearing throughout my stay: the Puerto Rican spindalis, a small, yellow-bellied bird native to the island.

The forest is also home to a seemingly endless variety of tropical trees, mushrooms, orchids, and ferns. Climb the spiral staircase of the Yokahú Observation Tower for panoramic views of the lush green canopy and surrounding mountain peaks, and be sure to pack water shoes if you fancy a refreshing dip in one of the forest’s rivers or natural waterfall pools.

Whether you’re an avid golfer or just getting into the sport, Río Grande has several world-class courses worth exploring. Among them is Bahía Beach Golf Club, an 18-hole, par-72 course designed by renowned golf course architect Robert Trent Jones Jr. in 2008. Stretching 6,890 yards through lush tropical landscapes, the course features 15 holes bordering water, with beautiful rainforest views along the way. You’ll wind around scenic lakes before reaching the Atlantic coastline for the final few holes, making for an unforgettable morning or afternoon on the green.

Set sail from the nearby town of Fajardo for a morning, afternoon, or all-day affair spent exploring nearby islands with seemingly untouched beaches. Popular destinations include Culebra and Icacos Island, where you can lounge on the boat, soak up the sun, swim in crystal-clear waters, or snorkel among vibrant coral reefs teeming with colorful fish.

Perla, located at Four Seasons, opened this November under the direction of executive chef Victor Rosado and became one of my favorite dining spots during my visit. Taking its name from the Spanish word for “pearl,” the elegant restaurant offers a tempting selection of small bites, from pillowy Parker House rolls served with smoked butter to spicy salmon mousse, alongside standout seafood dishes like hamachi and Chilean sea bass.

The thoughtfully designed interior boasts natural wood accents and bold contemporary artwork, with sweeping ocean views to admire between courses. As for what to order, don’t miss the oyster brûlée with yuzu kosho hollandaise and crispy Ibérico ham, the prime New York strip steak served with Hasselback potatoes, or the tender octopus accompanied by creamy potato causa.

For lunch, head to Don Pepe, a longtime local favorite where the atmosphere is casual and the focus is on authentic Puerto Rican cooking made with quality ingredients and bold flavors. The menu spans traditional favorites like beef piononos and mofongo served with your choice of protein and sauce, alongside heartier, mouthwatering dishes like succulent grilled pork loin, the restaurant’s signature burger, and lobster risotto. The extensive cocktail menu also offers a tempting selection of tropical concoctions made with locally produced Don Q rum.

Another recent addition to the dining options at the Four Seasons Resort is Ocean Terrace, a picturesque open-air restaurant set along the shoreline. Open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, the restaurant has a varied menu with something to satisfy every craving.

Mornings begin with a generous breakfast buffet, and if you have a sweet tooth like me, the coquito French toast on the à la carte menu is a must-try. For lunch, you’ll find everything from truffle honey stracciatella served with ciabatta to salads, pizzas, and sandwiches. Come dinnertime, I’d recommend exploring the selection of freshly made pastas, especially the creamy carbonara with pancetta—a dish I’m still dreaming about.

When you’re in the mood for a glamorous, atmospheric lounge to sip cocktails, head to Palm Court. The sleek, modern interior features plush seating that invites you to settle in and unwind, while a grand, square-shaped white marble bar serves as the room’s centerpiece. Beyond the elegant interior, an outdoor terrace offers additional seating for those who prefer to dine or enjoy a drink in the warm ocean breeze.

Located at the Bahía Beach Club, Sugar Beach Bar is a laid-back, open-air spot serving flavorful cocktails and delicious shareable bites. Sip on a tasty tropical cocktail made with local rum or tequila while soaking up stunning views of the ocean waves and Sugar Beach Pool.

Situated right by the Bahía Beach driving range, El Cocoteros Grill is a casual spot to unwind with a local beer. Open for breakfast and lunch, the restaurant offers a relaxed atmosphere, modern furnishings, and scenic rainforest views. And if you’re out on the golf course, you can even have drinks delivered straight to your golf cart.

You can always count on a five-star stay at a Four Seasons, and the recently opened Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, nestled within the picturesque Bahía Beach community, is no exception. Set across 483 acres of spectacular tropical landscape, the resort boasts 104 guest rooms, 35 luxurious suites, and an impressive collection of private residences. The property has rightfully earned a coveted Michelin Key in recognition of its exceptional grounds, hospitality, and dining.

The accommodations are everything you’d expect from the hotel company, with luxe, modern furnishings, 24-hour in-room dining, and an attentive concierge team that can arrange everything from dinner reservations to rainforest excursions. The location also doubles as a private nature reserve, with conservation efforts that include rain gardens and sea turtle nesting protection. Guests can explore the surrounding wildlife and tropical flora through guided nature experiences, all without leaving the vicinity. And if you find yourself wishing you could stay a little longer, the dreamy private residences offer a more permanent escape to paradise.

As for how to spend your days, take your pick among lounging along the resort’s two miles of pristine beachfront, cooling off in one of the two swimming pools, or heading out to explore the island.

A golf lover’s dream, Bahía Beach Resort & Golf Club offers a more residential take on the traditional resort experience. Visitors can enjoy a private getaway in one of the community’s luxurious villas and residences, many of which are available for short-term rentals. Among them is Paradise View Villa, an incredible two-bedroom, three-bathroom property that comes with a six-passenger golf cart for getting around the grounds. Guests also have access to an array of resort amenities, including the golf club, tennis facilities, a fitness center, and the Lakehouse, where a variety of water sports await.

Ideal for families, larger groups, or those planning a special celebration, Wyndham Grand Rio Mar has 400 guest rooms, including 40 spacious suites with refined, colorful furnishings. With so much to see and do on the property, you could easily spend your entire getaway without venturing beyond the resort. Indulge in restorative treatments at El Yunque Spa, spend a lazy afternoon under the sun on the beach, or enjoy a round of golf at the scenic Rio Mar Country Club.

#6663. 44 Best Wedding Guest Dresses in 2026 for Every Type of Ceremony

Once you’ve coordinated your wedding guest schedule, the next step is figuring out what to wear to all those nuptials. Between decoding dress codes (just how casual is a “casual” wedding, really?) and navigating different climates, you’ll quickly realize there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to this sort of occasion styling. So if you find yourself in the run-up to a fancy affair with a closet full of not-quite-right frocks and a looming deadline—don’t panic. We pulled together an edit of the best wedding guest dresses to suit every possible style, venue, and budget.

While some eveningwear requirements are set in stone, many leave room for creativity depending on the wedding theme. For instance: A black-tie ceremony does necessitate floor-length gowns—but that doesn’t mean a fuchsia-hued dress is off the table. A spring or summer wedding might have you gravitating toward sleeveless silhouettes and airier fabrics in the name of practicality, so why not pick a rich color like chartreuse or cerulean for an unexpected twist on the palette of the season? And while a cocktail dress code or daytime fête definitely suggests more laid-back attire, there’s plenty of opportunity to stand out with the details—think, a lace-trimmed midi or a tiger stripe-inspired number.

Whatever’s in the cards (we mean this literally—please read the invite carefully), our picks for the best wedding guest dresses cover a lot of ground.

The coldest days of the year come with the quandary of formal dressing for freezing temps (is there anything worse than having to cover a great dress with a puffer coat?). Stay warm in Staud’s long-sleeve maxi or a velvet option by Veronica Beard. Or, fully embrace winter glam in Simkhai’s halterneck gown, which has a low back for some drama.

Formal weddings are your moment to go all out with dramatic lengths and unexpected draping. Labels like Victoria Beckham, Fforme, and L’Agence show us how it’s done—just don’t forget the right jewels for a finishing touch.

Spring nuptials call for soft hues—though we’re all for trying a zippier take on pastels. H&M’s floral jacquard maxi dress in light turquoise will get you in the mood for a garden affair, while Totême’s soft pink midi pretty much works for any venue, as far as we’re concerned.

Toast the new couple in a spirited cocktail dress. COS’s gray midi delivers modern Art Deco glamour, while Ralph Lauren’s mock-neck style is all easy elegance. Then there’s Diotima’s LBD, a halterneck design bound to become a closet staple for future events.

Attending a courthouse ceremony or a more intimate backyard celebration? Elevated comfort is the name of the game. Slip on something easygoing with a modern finish—like Blaze Milano’s satin dress in a golden hue—or go for a more striking, unexpected piece from Tory Burch for a look that’s both playful and polished.

The best way to bring personality to a dress code with a limited palette? Play with silhouette and texture. Aje keeps things party-ready with fringe detailing; Kallmeyer brings evening elegance with a floor-length hem; and Banana Republic’s high-neck, long-sleeve option suits wintry affairs well.

This is one prompt that eliminates the guesswork; plus, you can never go wrong with a romantic bloom, no matter the silhouette. Keep accessories simple (sleek kitten heels and minimalist jewelry are the right choice here) and let the pattern do all the work.

From Italian villas to rolling countrysides, the best way to go about a destination wedding is to take notes from your surroundings. Lean into the romance of a cobblestoned town with a silky, lace-trimmed dress from Simon Miller, or buy into the breezy style of an island venue with Christopher John Rogers’ striped crinkle-chiffon gown.

Bold citrus hues and sultry silks define the mood for summer wedding dressing, we say—and Aflalo and Tove are both on board. For a more formal option, Taller Marmo’s one-shoulder gown with a fringe-trimmed cape will make you the best-dressed guest.

A shoreside ceremony is your cue to relax a little. Lighter-weight fabrics and simple silhouettes are fair game, especially when you play with texture and pattern. Coastal shades and sun-washed hues feel perfectly at home here, too. Style yours with open-toed sandals and nautical-inspired accessories, and you’re good to go.

Autumn wedding season calls for dresses in a deep, rich palette. La Ligne’s long-sleeve design in navy and Anine Bing’s modern slip in burgundy both offer universally flattering colors, while Maria McManus’s lace bodice dress and Dries Van Noten’s floral midi are splashier options for those with an affinity for details. Complete the look with a silk wrap draped around your shoulders once temperatures dip after cocktail hour.

When in doubt, let the season lead—jewel tones and deep neutrals for fall and winter, and soft pastels or vibrant hues for spring and summer. Be sure to also check the invitation and wedding website, as some couples may ask guests to dress within a color palette, and it’s important you honor their wishes.

What colors should I avoid as a wedding guest?

If you remember anything, remember this: Steer clear of white, ivory, and anything that could read as bridal, unless the couple says otherwise. Keep cultural customs in mind, too, as red and black are off-limits at some ceremonies. Again, if you’re unsure, check the invitation or wedding website, or ask a member of the bridal party for guidance.

How do I know what style and silhouette to wear?

The dress code, venue, season, and time of day should guide your choices. Here’s a quick rundown: Floor-length for black tie, knee- to midi-length for semi-formal and cocktail, minis for more casual celebrations, airy silhouettes for outdoor, beach, or daytime affairs, and thicker fabrics for the cooler months. And don’t forget about your accessories, whether that’s block heels for a lawn ceremony or a shawl for a more conservative house of worship.

How do I find a dress that works for multiple weddings?

If you have several weddings on the horizon, opt for a look in a solid hue and an easygoing shape, like a sheath style or handkerchief hemline. These pieces are extremely versatile, easier to rewear than trend-driven prints, and simple to restyle with different shoes, jewelry, and outerwear.

#6662. JFK Jr.’s ’94 Saab Is Up for Auction. You Should Buy It

The late John F. Kennedy Jr., in addition to being the subject of countless menswear moodboards, a hit Ryan Murphy series, and, hey, a new coffee table book written by yours truly, was one of the most stylish guys in 1990s New York. Between his American-dynasty pedigree, chiseled good looks, and impossibly thick head of hair, not to mention his eclectic wardrobe of preppy classics, funky gorpcore, and Armani suits, it’s not hard to see why. It should come as no surprise, then, that he also had excellent taste in cars. Throughout the ’90s, JFK Jr.’s whip of choice was a 1994 Saab 900 SE Coupe, a quirky Swedish sports car that embodied everything that was great about ’90s style, down to its hunter green paint. Fortunately, for fans of oddball vintage autos and JFK Jr. alike, it’s currently up for sale via RR Auction, and the bids are rolling in.

Sporty, sophisticated, and eccentric, the Saab 900 was to JFK Jr. what the pink Cadillac Fleetwood was to Elvis, or the Porsche 935 was to Paul Newman. An consummate outlier in the American car market since the ’50s, Saab’s popularity peaked in the mid-1980s when its weird, angular designs and quirks(e.g., the ignition was next to the handbrake) found a following among design-obsessed American yuppies. Combining the Scandinavian sobriety of a Volvo with the postmodern flair of a Memphis sofa, Saab loomed large in ’90s culture: Jerry Seinfeld’s TV alter-ego drove one, as did Niles Crane, Dana Scully, and Clark Griswald’s humorless neighbors in National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation.

During the tail end of the decade, when JFK Jr. and his late wife, publicist Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, were fixtures of Lower Manhattan life, the couple was frequently photographed driving in the Saab near their Tribeca loft. With its sporty-yet-economical turbocharged four-cylinder engine, a sleek leather interior, and a custom set of aftermarket aqua-blue padded ski racks mounted to the roof, it embodied JFK Jr.’s characteristic blend of aristocratic, athletic, and bohemian to a tee.

JFK Jr.'s green 1994 Saab 900 SE, with a current bid of nearly $30,000 and rising.

According to Bobby Livingston, executive vice president at RR Auction, “what makes this lot so special is it's not some Maserati or something flashy like that—it's a practical car that was a part of his everyday life. For Kennedy, “the choice of this car, as opposed to a Mercedes or something, speaks a lot to his style.” This particular Saab—which JFK Jr. purchased new from Zumbach Sports Cars in Manhattan for $29,841.21 in the summer of 1994, and owned until his death in 1999—comes to auction via Kevin J. Hynes, a screenwriter and longtime friend of Kennedy’s who worked with him at the New York DA’s office in the early ’90s. According to the auction listing, the car had been left at Hynes’s Westchester home in the days following Kennedy’s fatal plane crash. In 2000, Hynes then bought the car from the Kennedy estate in 2000 for $6,000, and sold it for $12,000 two years later. Its third owner is said to have started up the car regularly, but judging by its overall condition and the looks of its odometer, which shows just 30,650 miles, it seems it hasn’t hit the road in a long time.

The Saab, which was listed with a minimum sale price of $15,000, is part of a RR’s Fine Autographs and Artifacts auction that also includes a tweed hat worn by the elder JFK and Lee Harvey Oswald’s overcoat. As of Wednesday afternoon, more than 20 bids have driven the price close to $30,000. “We’ve sold a Hummer that belonged to Tupac, and a Cadillac Escalade that was used by Tony Soprano in The Sopranos, but I didn't know there would be such an affection for John F. Kennedy Jr.’s Saab,” says Livingston. “It’s already exceeded our estimate, and there’s a lot of interest, so it could go for a lot more than where it is right now.”

The Kennedys, seen here in 1998, were frequently seen driving in the Saab near their Tribeca loft.

Given its provenance and climbing auction price tag, whether JFK Jr.’s Saab ends up with a car collector, a Kennedy buff, or someone with a keen appreciation for peak-1990s style, one hopes that whoever buys it will be well-equipped to give it the treatment it deserves. That is to say, this is a car that deserves to be street-parked in Tribeca, driven to Vermont for ski trips, and otherwise treated like the ’90s style icon it is. A backward Kangol cap and an “I TOLD YA” tee are optional, but highly recommended.

#6661. I Tried Keurig’s First-Ever Espresso Machine—Is It Worth Adding To Your Coffee Routine?

I’ve owned a Keurig, I’ve owned a Nespresso, and I’ve spent way too much money on coffee shop runs in between. Needless to say, I’m an expert on the subject. So when I heard that Keurig was launching its first-ever espresso machine, my interest was piqued. Could the brand that turned single-serve coffee into the household standard successfully switch up its game?

Keurig’s latest and possibly greatest innovation—a two-in-one single-serve coffee maker and espresso machine called the Alta System—will turn your home kitchen into a coffee shop thanks to a multifunctional design that brews everything from regular coffee to espresso, cappuccinos, and lattes. It comes with a built-in milk frother and functions exclusively on the new plastic- and aluminum-free pods (sustainability, hallelujah!).

Here’s whether the Keurig Alta System lives up to the hype, how it compares to other machines, and whether it deserves a spot on your own kitchen coffee bar.

Let’s go a little more in-depth, shall we? The Keurig Alta System is the brand’s new single-serve coffee and espresso machine that does a lot more than your standard K-Cup brewer. Unlike the brand’s traditional lineup, which uses K-Cup pods, the Alta introduces an entirely new innovation: AltaRounds. Your machine can read a code on the AltaRounds and adjust its brew settings accordingly, whether that’s pressure, temperature, or the water-to-coffee ratio. (K-Cups are still compatible with the Alta).

The integrated milk frother is another major upgrade for Keurig, letting you make hot and cold foam.

The Keurig Alta System is $499.99, which, yes, is pricier than other Keurig models. However, classic espresso machines can run you upwards of $1,000.

As for the AltaRounds, they’re sold in boxes of eight, ranging from $9.99 to $10.99 depending on the variety. If you wanna break that up by coffee, it’s about $1.25 to $1.37 a cup. Not too shabby.

As someone who is impatient and terrible at reading directions (hello, your type B friend reporting for duty), I wasn’t overly optimistic I’d figure it out that quickly. But it’s actually an easy device to navigate, thanks to the convenient LED screen that walks you through the whole process.

I was immediately transfixed by the machine. I texted my boyfriend, “I’m in love with it,” before it even finished brewing my first coffee. The Alta feels so much chicer on my countertops, and the pods are smaller and store more easily. Once I finally took that first sip, I was ready to toss my old Keurig in the trash (respectfully).

The drip coffee and espresso shots taste like something straight from an award-winning barista. I love the flexibility to make a black coffee one day and an iced caramel latte the next. And the milk frother just takes the entire thing to the next level.

Listen, $500 for a coffee machine is a lot. And maybe because of that, this isn’t an upgrade you can make immediately. Still, the Keurig Alta System is worth the hype; if you can swap your classic single-serve maker for it, you should. It checks literally every box—it’s more aesthetic, more versatile, and more sustainable.

The only caveat is if you’re the type of person who exclusively drinks drip coffee. In that case, it might not be worth the splurge. But if you want to cosplay as a barista and whip up new creations, from frothy cappuccinos to iced lattes and espresso martinis, the Alta provides all the room to experiment (and it will ultimately save you money on those $10 coffee runs).

#6659. 26 Best Men's Scarves 2026, According to GQ Editors

Are any accessories as essential, yet mysteriously overlooked, as the best men's scarves? First, they warm your neck (and face, and chest) like nothing else. Second, they put a style-forward, cheery, colorful bow on pretty much any outfit. And yet, these soft little miracles are all too often an afterthought in the menswear world. Even if you’re the type of guy to painstakingly lay your fits out the night before, chances are when it comes to your scarf game, you’re still reaching for one you picked up in a rushed pinch from Nordstrom Rack, or at a frigid college football game.

This is, of course, fine. But it’s also sort of a tragedy. Because when you pick up a truly great scarf, everything changes. Swaddling your neck in cashmere (or cashmere-emulating fabrics) doesn’t just provide a soothing all-day embrace through bracing winds. It also, like a necktie, creates an opportunity for a flash of personal style, right under your handsome face. Even better, because scarves use less fabric than coats and knitwear, they’re also a great way to own some of the best materials in our industry for far less scratch.

To help you pick the one you’ll soon be recognized by, I surveyed hundreds of scarves from across the fashion (and budget) spectrum, journeying from mall chains, to historic British manufacturers, to the buzziest makers today, and everything in-between. Below, the final 26 best men's scarves to knot up this winter—and next winter, and the one after that.

Parisian label Brut puts a Big Apple spin on the classic European football supporter scarf, featuring none other than Lady Liberty herself. A fitting French connection.

The bandana, neckerchief, foulard, whatever you want to call it has become an easy, even trendy winter accessory. Alex Mill’s is made from extra-fine merino wool, comes in 14 colors, and costs less than a hundo.

Another bandana-shaped style from the Banana, this time with a generous helping of cashmere for a little extra softness.

A smart tartan plaid as classic as the linings inside Barbour’s famous wax jackets, in a soft wool-cashmere blend. About as British as a rainy afternoon and a pint at the pub.

We cross the Irish Sea for L.L.Bean’s take, made from Irish-woven lambswool, known for its durability and natural water resistance. Plenty warm and handsome to boot.

Lost & Found’s Scottish lambswool scarf comes with pockets stitched into it. Perfect for stashing your cards, cash or other things a little less above board. We won’t ask.

On the GORP-ier side of things, this thermal fleece scarf balances warmth, stretch and lightweight comfort in a slimmed-down design that will both fit with your puffer and stay out of your way.

Quince has made a name for itself selling luxury materials at un-luxury prices. Case in point: this soft scarf made from 100% Mongolian cashmere, at a price you could get two with.

Another triangle scarf, here in a stunning sienna color that’s still right in Margaret Howell’s wheelhouse. Snug and sensible.

Lil’ brown checks, a fuzzy brushed finish, and Japanese cotton-wool twill woven in England. A big helping of understated charm.

A nice change of pace from the usual winter plaids, two-tone chevrons give this Coach scarf a little graphic punch, while a lightweight but warm alpaca blend keeps things cosy.

If you love pattern, fall and winter is primed for Polo Power. This Fair-Isle-esque design is easier to wear than the classic sweater, and will add some energy to your winter fits.

True to form, Kapital keeps things weird with a wild leopard-and-paisley design. The lightweight gauze also means you can wear it a dozen different ways, pretty much any time of year.

William Lockie’s scarves will set you back a few extra bucks, but they’ve been at it since 1874, so you're buying proven scarf smarts. In this case: Pure cashmere, traditional techniques, and even a pre-sale bath in local fresh water for added softness.

Todd Snyder isn’t reinventing the wheel here, this is just a beautifully brushed cashmere scarf. Classic, timeless, soft, and warm as they come.

Howlin’ often brings a little irreverence to its sweaters, and the same goes for its scarves. Here, throwback collegiate “fun” stripes show the brand’s take on the Ivy scarves of yesteryear.

Made from Italian wool, this Mfpen number gives you two checks for the price of one, thanks to a clever double-faced design. Twist it, drape it, wear it however you please.

All the cozy, old-school charm of an Aran knit, Percival takes the classic cream cable-knit sweater and turns it into a scarf. And at more than half off, it’s a bit of a steal.

She's pricey, but you’re paying for fine Scottish-spun cashmere materials and serious know-how with an entirely handmade and hand-linked scarf.

Printed scarves were the first things Drake’s made back in 1977, when it was still a small workshop. These archival designs are works of art you can wear. Wool, silk and good taste.

Missoni’s famous zigzags came out of swinging ’60s Milan, and they still have that groovy Italian charm. Funny how something so unmistakably of its time never seems to go out of style.

A statement scarf if there ever was one, with vibrant Yves Klein blue and an oversized logo patch that’s not shy about announcing itself. A lot to spend on yourself, maybe, but one hell of a gift.

There’s something dashingly medieval about a shearling scarf. Wrap it around your neck for a bit of Feudal-Lord-core. Beats a suit of armor.

NN07 mixes two old-school patterns into one elegant Italian-woven scarf, with a fuzzy brushed finish and blanket-stitched edges. Your granddad would approve.

This fashion-guy-approved cashmere scarf from Auralee is classic enough, but boy, those rich colours are doing something for me. It truly is all in the details.

By now, you may have noticed the Scots know a thing or two about wool. Johnstons of Elgin has been at it for centuries, and this beautifully woven cashmere scarf is further proof.

#6658. Nanofat Is Dermatologists’ Best-Kept Secret for Younger, Fresher Skin

It’s not an injectable filler, and it’s not fat transfer. It’s a secret third thing you’ll want to try.

The last few years have been unkind to our facial fat. We sliced out our buccal pads to create sunken-in, razor-sharp cheekbones. We zapped our skin with thermal devices that accidentally melted fat away in pursuit of boosting collagen. We injected our stomachs with fat-loss GLP-1 medications, leaving our faces looking hollow. Droopy. Structurally unsound. As it turns out, facial fat is critical infrastructure—not just for looking younger, but for your skin's overall health and quality. And while you can’t choose where you lose or gain fat, you can choose to have a doctor siphon it, remix it, and reinject it.

“Adipose tissue is a rich source of growth factors and progenitor cells, and re-injecting fat is probably one of the best ways to regenerate the full potential of healthy skin I've seen in the last decades,” says Patricia Ogilvie, a Munich-based dermatologist and member of the Dior Reverse Aging Board. “There are trends that are not really worth being a trend. I think the restaging of the importance of adipose tissue is very justified.”

You’re probably familiar with fat transfer, a procedure that’s been around for decades. In simple terms, fat transfer takes adipose tissue from one area of your body, like your flanks, liposuctions it, and moves it to another area, like your breasts or cheekbones. “With traditional fat transfer, it’s about restoring volume. And because it’s your own living tissue, it can integrate beautifully and give you very natural-looking results,” says dermatologist Sheerene Idriss, medical director and founder of Idriss Dermatology in New York City. “But what’s interesting is that fat isn’t just fat. It also contains regenerative cells, including adipose-derived stem cells, and growth factors that may help improve the surrounding tissue over time. Nanofat is where it gets really exciting.”

Nanofat is part of a new class of regenerative aesthetics offered by dermatologists and plastic surgeons, treatments that don’t just make you look better, but rather address the signs of aging from the inside out by stimulating collagen or repairing tissue. Imagine taking that same fat from a traditional fat transfer and processing it into a fine, milky liquid rich in your own stem cells and growth factors, then injecting or microneedling it back into your face—that’s nanofat.

“Instead of using it to restore volume, you’re using it to potentially improve skin quality itself,” says Idriss. “These cells and growth factors communicate with surrounding tissue and can stimulate processes involved in collagen production, tissue repair, and blood vessel formation. So you’re not just trying to fill a wrinkle. You’re trying to improve the skin itself—its thickness, resilience, and texture—so that wrinkle potentially becomes less noticeable.”

The best areas for nanofat injections include under the eye, a notoriously risky area for hyaluronic acid fillers, and the cheekbones. “The ideal patient for nanofat is someone who's starting to notice thinner, crepier skin, fine lines, or changes in skin texture, especially around the eyes, neck, or chest, and wants to improve skin quality rather than add volume,” adds Idriss, who both has had the treatment done and offers it in her practice. Plus, Ogilvie notes, nanofat doesn’t attract water the way fillers do, so it won’t cause under-eye puffiness (a common post-filler complaint). But because nanofat doesn’t restore volume as much as it reinvigorates your skin, you can inject it almost anywhere you’re noticing signs of aging.

“We do it under tumescent local anesthesia, so you’re awake the entire time, and recovery is usually pretty quick,” says Idriss. “I personally had nanofat and fat transfer in June and was back at work the next day. The biggest downside is some soreness at the fat extraction site, which usually lasts a few days, and you’ll want to avoid strenuous exercise for about a week. Because there’s no general anesthesia, you’re also avoiding the grogginess and recovery associated with being put under.”

Like any cosmetic treatment, it has risks and downsides. Experts note that nanofat isn’t the right treatment for anyone looking to restore significant volume loss or seeking instant results. “Improvement in skin quality can vary from person to person, and it takes months to see the full results,” Idriss adds. “There are rare but serious risks, including infection, vascular complications, and even vision loss when injecting certain areas of the face.” But patients who have tried the procedure say the recovery is quick and easy, with results compounding over weeks, though they ultimately fade away faster than traditional injectables.

Nanofat injections sit somewhere between microfat and hyaluronic acid fillers. Microfat can be lumpy and unpredictable when injected, sometimes leading to lopsided results. Plus, in any fat transfer, only a small amount of fat survives. Fillers, on the other hand, offer long-lasting precision and volume restoration, but patients are tired of looking overfilled and unnaturally plump. Nanofat helps your skin look naturally healthier, fresher, and firmer, at least for a while. After all, it’s made from you.

“I look at this as something you can do periodically throughout your life, but what you do in between treatments is just as important. And that’s why I don’t believe in demonizing any one treatment, including filler,” says Idriss. “When used appropriately, for the right indication, these treatments can all work beautifully together. It’s about knowing what you need, when you need it, and when enough is enough.”

#6657. Safe Word: The Best Jewelry Launches of November 2026

Safe Word is a series highlighting the latest trends in the jewelry market, keeping you up to date on all things that sparkle and shine.

November’s jewelry launches are looking both backward and forward, with designers revisiting their roots, reworking archival ideas, and stepping into entirely new territory. First up, Quentin Jones is taking her surrealist art off the wall and onto the body with ‘Nocturne’, her first jewelry collection; Pomellato reaches back to 1997 to revive “Moneta Orientale” as a colorful modern talisman; David Yurman celebrates the magic of a New York holiday with Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette; Vhernier revisits its iconic “Trottola” design with new proportions and contrasting materials; Di Volpe reinterprets the classic tennis bracelet with customizable gemstones in “DiSegno”; Brent Neale transforms the classic bow into sculptural fine jewelry with “Wrap It Up”; and Kendra Scott launches the new “Kendra Scott Collection,” reimagining her signature Spike motif as a personal talisman. From archival revivals and meaningful motifs to innovative designs and new creative directions, November’s launches prove that sometimes the best way forward starts with looking back. For the rest of the month, we’ve got you covered on all the jewelry-related happenings worth knowing about.

Quentin Jones is taking her art off the wall and onto the body with “Nocturne,” the first jewelry collection from House of Quentin Jones. Following the multidisciplinary artist’s debut of surrealist ceramics and tapestries last year, the new collection transforms recurring gestures and symbols from her work into sculptural collars, cuffs, armbands, pendants, chains, and earrings. Eyes, hands, stars, moons, tears, and knots take shape in silver and gold vermeil alongside freshwater pearls, onyx, opals, jade, glass, and silk tassels, giving the pieces a dreamlike, talismanic quality. Beginning as drawings and hand collages in Jones’s Brooklyn studio, each design carries her surrealist visual language into wearable form, further blurring the line between art, design, and fashion.

Kendra Scott Launches an Eponymous Collection

Kendra Scott is offering a more personal look into her design world with the launch of the “Kendra Scott Collection,” a new line spanning fashion and fine jewelry. Its first edition, “The Spike,” revisits a silhouette the designer has worn throughout her career as a personal symbol of strength, confidence, and conviction. Inspired by nature and the radiance of the night sky, the collection translates the pointed motif into sculptural necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and charms, balancing bold proportions with intricate craftsmanship. Fashion jewelry incorporates tiger’s eye, malachite, and turquoise, while fine jewelry introduces lab-grown diamonds, pavé detailing, labradorite, and lapis. From statement-making links to delicate diamond charms, the collection offers a new interpretation of Scott’s longtime signature, inviting wearers to make the symbol their own.

Alison Lou’s ‘New Wave’ Collection Experiments With New Materials

Alison Lou is entering a new chapter with “New Wave,” a fine jewelry collection that introduces unexpected materials and a fresh approach to the designer’s signature playful aesthetic. Exploring the relationship between movement and form, the collection pairs lightweight titanium and ceramic with lab-grown diamonds, creating fluid, sculptural silhouettes that curve and catch the light. Available in Fig and Denim Blue colorways, the designs include wavy rings, diamond-accented signets, delicate thread necklaces, and statement drop earrings. With its unconventional materials and easy-to-wear designs, “New Wave” brings a new sense of movement to Alison Lou’s everyday jewelry.

Jenny Bird and Emese Gormley Partner on the Anyu Ring

Jenny Bird is expanding her JB FINE collection with a new collaboration featuring lifestyle creator and Lipstick on the Rim podcast host Emese Gormley. Named in honor of Gormley’s mother, the Anyu Ring offers a personal take on the classic signet, featuring three lab-grown baguette diamonds set in 14-karat yellow or white gold. The understated design combines the timeless appeal of a signet ring with a sentimental tribute to family, bringing a new perspective to Bird’s growing fine jewelry offering. Available exclusively on Jenny Bird’s website, the collaboration makes a case for jewelry that feels as meaningful as it looks.

Pomellato Revives Its 1997 Moneta Orientale Pendant as a Colorful Talisman

Pomellato is looking to its archives for its latest good-luck charm. For the newest chapter of “Memorie d’Archivio,” the maison revives Moneta Orientale, a 1997 pendant inspired by the ancient symbolism of a circle surrounding a square, representing the harmony between heaven and earth. Made in 33 stone-and-pavé combinations, the design pairs colorful hard stones including black jade, amazonite, sodalite, rhodochrosite, and labradorite with Pomellato’s signature irregular pavé of diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and more. Offered in two proportions, each pendant transforms the archival motif into a modern talisman for prosperity and protection.

Bibi van der Velden Makes Her High Jewelry Debut With ‘Eclipse’

Bibi van der Velden is entering a new era with “Eclipse,” the designer’s first high jewelry collection and most refined exploration of diamonds to date. Inspired by the fleeting moment when light gives way to darkness, the collection includes two six-piece suites: one in white diamonds and another defined by an ombré of diamonds into gray spinels deepening into black. Van der Velden’s signature alligator motif is abstracted into fluid, sculptural silhouettes, with scales engraved into the white gold on the reverse of each piece. “With Eclipse, I wanted to take those familiar elements and transform them into something more abstract and sculptural,” she says. “It’s a collection about transformation, which has always been at the heart of my work.”

Aflalo and Leandra Medine Cohen Turn Everyday Indulgences Into Fine Jewelry

Aflalo is finding the humor in our obsession with wellness with “The Vanities,” a new two-piece fine jewelry capsule designed exclusively by Leandra Medine Cohen. Playing with the contradiction between longevity and life’s little indulgences, the collection transforms two unlikely everyday accessories into precious objects. The Memento Mori is a 14-karat yellow gold cigar band set with more than four carats of diamonds, designed to slip over an Oura Ring, while The Libertine is a sterling silver pendant case adorned with diamonds and a wild-haired woman outlined in gold, designed to hold nicotine pouches or other small essentials. Equal parts extravagant and irreverent, the collection makes a playful case for enjoying life’s pleasures without sacrificing personal style.

Julia Berolzheimer’s Hart Jewelry Collection Draws on Childhood Memories

Hart is teaming up with Julia Berolzheimer for a new jewelry collection that celebrates the art of the stack. Inspired by Berolzheimer’s childhood memories of her grandmother’s California ranch and her collection of Art Deco minaudières, the collaboration brings together whimsical charms, colorful gemstones, and meaningful talismans designed to be mixed, layered, and restyled. Botanical motifs take shape in Tree of Life coins, daisies, bees, and fruit-inspired charms, while carnelian, turquoise, and pink opal add playful pops of color. One standout is the Perfume Vesta Case, a modern interpretation of a Victorian-era accessory that can hold a sample-sized fragrance and hang alongside other charms. With interchangeable chains, cords, and pendants, the collection makes a case for jewelry that feels just as personal as the memories behind it.

David Yurman Captures the Magic of a New York Holiday

David Yurman is celebrating the magic of the holidays in New York City with a new campaign featuring global brand ambassador Michael B. Jordan alongside actresses Yerin Ha and Inde Navarrette. Set against a snow-covered Washington Square Park, the campaign captures a series of quintessential New York moments, from Jordan and Ha facing off in a spirited card game to Navarrette hailing a cab in search of the perfect holiday gift. Throughout the campaign, the cast wears some of the house’s most recognizable designs, including 18-karat gold Cable bracelets and pieces from the “Starburst” and “Armory” collections. Directed by Bradford Young and photographed by Drew Vickers, the campaign brings together the spirit of the city, the joy of togetherness, and the timeless appeal of David Yurman’s jewelry.

Vhernier Reintroduces Its Iconic ‘Trottola’ Design With New Proportions

Vhernier is revisiting one of its most recognizable designs with a new interpretation of “Trottola,” the sculptural collection originally introduced in 2003. Inspired by the continuous motion of a spinning top, the latest designs play with proportions, contrasting materials, and asymmetrical shapes across rings, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Polished rose gold meets glossy black jet, with select pieces featuring diamond pavé for an added contrast of light and dark. The collection also focuses on versatility, from rings designed for stacking to convertible earclips that can be worn as studs or dangling earrings. With its fluid forms and unexpected material combinations, “Trottola” brings a fresh perspective to Vhernier’s signature sculptural approach to jewelry.

Di Volpe is rethinking the classic tennis bracelet with “DiSegno,” a new customizable fine jewelry system designed to change with its wearer. Using concealed, patent-pending connections, individual cultured diamonds and gemstones, called Elements, can be removed, rearranged, or added by hand, allowing wearers to transform bracelets into necklaces or earrings without compromising the seamless look of traditional tennis jewelry. The collection launches with 28 stone-and-cut combinations, including rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and diamonds, alongside a limited-edition collaboration with Lebanese artist Ali Cha’aban featuring five sculptural designs. With new cuts, colors, and artist collaborations planned for future releases, “DiSegno” makes the case for fine jewelry that’s never quite finished.

Brent Neale Riffs on the Bow in Fine Jewelry

Brent Neale is putting a bow on the holiday season with “Wrap It Up,” a new fine jewelry collection that transforms the familiar ribbon motif into sculptural works of art. Drawing inspiration from Old Hollywood glamour and the femininity of the 1960s, the designer plays with the contrast between rigid precious metals and the soft movement of fabric, crafting bows that twist, curl, and unfurl in 18-karat gold and platinum. Colored gemstones sit nestled within the ribbon-like forms, while pavé diamonds accentuate every curve and fold. Equal parts playful and precious, the collection brings a little gift-wrapped glamour to the jewelry box.

Grace Winfrey’s ‘Poppy Fortuna’ Collection Reimagines Good-Luck Charms

Grace Winfrey is bringing a little extra luck to the jewelry box with “Poppy Fortuna,” a new fine jewelry collection inspired by the natural beauty of the Italian landscape and symbols of good fortune. Scarlet poppies, sunflowers, bees, four-leaf clovers, horseshoes, and ladybugs come to life through vibrant gemstones and intricate pavé, creating miniature mosaics of color and texture. Highlights include a Lucky Bangle combining three good-luck charms, sculptural sunflower earrings with tiny ladybugs tucked into their petals, and layered charm necklaces designed to feel like modern keepsakes. Handcrafted in New York City, each piece transforms familiar symbols of prosperity, protection, and happiness into playful, colorful works of art.

Robinson Pelham Channels ’90s Glamour for Its Anniversary

Robinson Pelham is closing out its 30th anniversary celebrations with “Suite 96,” a new campaign and collection launch inspired by the glamour of late-’90s London. Set inside a private suite at St. James’s Hotel & Club in Mayfair, the campaign considers jewelry the ultimate room service, with diamonds arriving on trays, gold spilling out of wardrobes, and plenty of pieces to layer before a night out. At the center is “Studio 30,” a four-piece anniversary collection featuring diamond necklaces and statement earrings, including the sculptural Via and Hira necklaces, cascading diamond drops, and the bold Solstice Supreme. Alongside the anniversary designs, the house introduces new collections and additions to existing favorites, from chunky gold links and graphic heart rings to colorful enamel and gemstone combinations. Together, the launches celebrate three decades of Robinson Pelham’s bold, playful approach to fine jewelry.

Le Vian and Jared Revive Georgian-Era Romance

Le Vian is bringing a little old-world romance to Jared Jewelers with its new exclusive “Georgian Chocolate & Nude Diamonds” collection. Inspired by the candlelit jewels of the Georgian era, when jewelry was designed to capture and reflect the warmth of natural light, the collection rethinks historic buttercup settings in polished Honey Gold, with eight rounded prongs framing each natural diamond. The designs pair Le Vian’s signature Chocolate and Nude Diamonds with warm gold detailing across solitaire rings, anniversary bands, tennis bracelets, necklaces, and earrings. Select styles introduce colorful gemstones including Chocolate Quartz, Green Apple Peridot, and Grape Amethyst, giving the vintage-inspired silhouettes a contemporary update. With its sculptural settings and warm-toned stones, the collection brings the romance of antique jewelry into the present.

Wempe’s ‘Au:thentic’ Celebrates the Art of Goldsmithing

Wempe’s new gender-inclusive fine jewelry collection, “Au:thentic,” puts craftsmanship front and center, finding inspiration in the foundational skills taught to aspiring goldsmiths. The collection takes its shape from the jump ring, one of the first techniques Patrick Sieroslawski learned as an apprentice more than 22 years ago, translating its form to necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and pendants. Handcrafted at Wempe’s atelier in Germany, the pieces come in 18-karat yellow, white, and rose gold, with select styles set with diamonds. “Au:thentic” also marks the beginning of a multiyear rollout, with three additional chapters set to expand on its design language through twists, wraps, and interlocking links.

#6655. Who Will Be the Next-Gen Bond Girls? Here Are 45 Contenders

Who will be the next James Bond? With final screen tests having recently taken place, we may now be closer to an answer than ever before.

But when the news does come, attention will quickly turn to another pressing question: who will make up the next generation of Bond girls? Far from being the helpless ingénues of yore, under the direction of new Bond helmer Denis Villeneuve, we presume these women will be more than a match for 007—rival agents and worthy adversaries, perhaps, alongside the inevitable love interests. Here are 45 contenders who would fit the bill.

If her husband, Jack Lowden, does indeed become 007, could the Irish four-time Oscar nominee come aboard, too? They’d be very lucky to have her.

Post-Obsession, the 2027 Oscar hopeful has joined the MCU as Rogue in the next X-Men movie, so she’s clearly not opposed to blockbuster franchise work. As ridiculously talented newcomer-turned-overnight sensations go, she feels destined to be a Bond girl.

Having already collaborated with Denis Villeneuve on the Dune trilogy—not to mention being one of the most bankable actors working today—the fashion favorite should be at the front of the queue.

Like mother like daughter: back in 2015, Monica Bellucci was a Bond girl opposite Daniel Craig in Spectre. Could her 22-year-old progeny, a vision in Netflix’s recent ravishing period drama The Leopard, follow in her footsteps?

From Squid Game to the barnstorming new Korean monster movie Hope, the model-turned-actor has proved her chops and would be a worthy partner in crime for 007—particularly if the new plot line takes him east.

After collecting a number of big-screen credits—Erupcja, 100 Nights of Hero, The Moment, I Want Your Sex—would the Brit join the Bond franchise as a scintillating fellow secret agent? Hell, she could write the new song, too.

The Bridgerton breakout is a national treasure who’s long deserved a splashy big-screen part.

As a wisecracking foil to a somber Bond, who could be better than the Bottoms and The Bear star?

If Bond’s latest mission takes him to Scandinavia, it’s easy to see the Norwegian Oscar nominee and indie darling–best known for The Worst Person in the World, Sentimental Value, Backrooms, and now Fjord—joining him as a steely colleague.

The Mancunian Oscar nominee lit up the screen in Sinners and would do the same in any Bond movie.

Mosaku’s The Social Reckoning co-star, a recent Oscar winner, has been tipped as a potential Bond girl ever since her magnetic turn in Anora.

If Bond heads to the Indian subcontinent on his mission, might I suggest casting a Bollywood powerhouse and red-carpet regular with more than 85 million followers as his local liaison?

Having delivered wonderfully sensitive performances in everything from Waves to Bones and All, as well as on the National Theatre stage in The Effect, the Canadian actor would be a thoughtful, high-brow choice.

The chameleonic Past Lives star could be a quippy fellow agent (remember her in Russian Doll?) just as easily as she could morph into a terrifying villain.

Since Normal People, the Londoner has been ticking projects off her bucket list: she’s starred in a big-budget summer blockbuster (Twisters) and now played a Jane Austen heroine (Sense and Sensibility), so could taking the part of a Bond girl be next?

After her awards-laden run on Shōgun, the Japanese actor will be playing Yoko Ono in the four Beatles movies. If I had to put money on anyone snagging a Bond girl role, it’d be her.

Another Bridgerton fixture who’s since gone stratospheric, the Brit fits the classic Bond girl mold—impossibly beautiful and surprisingly steely (never forget her throwing punches in the Regency romp’s first season).

The One Day star is showing off her action-heroine chops on the second season of Black Doves opposite Keira Knightley. Could that act as an audition for a bigger big-screen part?

She played Carolyn Bessette Kennedy to widespread acclaim—slipping into a Bond girl’s stilettos feels like the obvious next move.

Her turn as Catwoman proved she’s a high-kicking, gun-toting force to be reckoned with. After that, being a Bond girl would surely be a walk in the park.

She’s an Oscar-nominated British A-lister, outstanding in everything from Lady Macbeth and Little Women to Midsommar and, recently, East of Eden. Need we say more?

With her winking sense of humor and laid-back glamour, it’d be a thrill to see the Vogue favorite as a Bond girl.

After One Battle After Another brought her to prominence, the American actor led Hulu’s The Testaments. A plum part as a Bond girl could be an ideal next step.

One of the most powerful actors and producers in Hollywood right now, the Australian is prime Bond girl material in every sense.

She leapt to the top of Bond girl leaderboards back in 2025, when she performed in a 007 tribute number at the Oscars. She’s been sensational in everything from Fosse/Verdon and Maid to The Substance, and certainly has the charisma to pull it off.

Another fashion favorite who ought to get a look-in is the Chicago-born star of BlacKkKlansman and Hollywood.

Could the Brit of House of the Dragon and The Girlfriend fame get Bond to trade in his vodka martini for a negroni… sbagliato… with prosecco in it? We think so.

If we need a madcap Bond girl to get 007 out of a bind, the Marty Supreme and I Love LA star feels like a safe bet.

We’re so ready for the Hustlers and Nope star to say “sorry to this man” to 007.

Now that Euphoria is over, the LA native is due her big-screen breakout moment.

Funny Bond girls were few and far between in the Daniel Craig era, but casting the Sex Education and The White Lotus breakout would be hearkening back to that tradition in classic Bond movies of the ’70s.

Another star of One Battle After Another who really should be considered is the very funny, always sharply dressed and extremely talented Oscar nominee.

Like Alexa Demie, the fashion stalwart has graduated from Euphoria and, despite parts in The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Kinds of Kindness, and Mother Mary, is still waiting for her big-screen movie star moment. A Bond girl role would be just the ticket.

After her stint on The Celebrity Traitors, the Industry star is at least an honorary Brit. Make her a Bond girl, stat.

Her extraordinary lead performance in How to Have Sex put her on the map, and she’ll soon be in the Beatles movies (as Ringo Starr’s first wife, Maureen Cox). The Brit feels ripe for another high-profile casting moment.

After Wednesday, could the Californian play a deadpan Bond girl next?

The Emma, The Queen’s Gambit, and Dune franchise star is another actor who feels like something of a no-brainer for the part of the next Bond girl.

The exceedingly gifted Londoner could easily go head-to-head with 007; just recall her sly turn in Prime Video’s Mr. and Mrs. Smith reboot.

A scene-stealer in the final season of Euphoria, she could bring the same flair and ferociousness to the Bond franchise. (She could pen the next Bond song, too!)

Another Industry alum who has the chops and innate glamour needed to pull off a Bond girl role is the captivating Brit.

Following the end of Stranger Things, the now-all-grown-up Texan could very well be in with a shot.

The Puerto Rico-born, Mexico City-raised actor charmed us as the sizzling femme fatale in Hit Man opposite Glen Powell—and seems set to do so again in Michael B. Jordan’s The Thomas Crown Affair. She would undoubtedly be a stellar foil for Bond.

From Yellowjackets to Heretic, Companion and Her Private Hell, the American actor has become her generation’s most sought-after steely scream queen—resilient, mesmeric, even deadly. Ideal qualities for a Bond girl, too, one could argue…

The Liverpudlian has herself played a notorious assassin in Killing Eve, meaning a match-up with Bond would be one for the ages.

She crooned her way into our hearts with (and earned an Oscar nod for) A Complete Unknown, and then romanced Bond frontrunner Callum Turner in One Night Only. If he’s officially cast as 007, could a reunion be imminent?

#6654. Sade Is No Ordinary Style Icon

An ode to the singer who was ahead of her time.

Has there ever been anyone as effortlessly ahead of her time as Sade? Born Helen Folasade Adu on Jan. 16, 1959, in Ibadan, Nigeria, the frontwoman of her namesake band has a core aesthetic that revolves around blindingly bright hoop earrings, a slicked-back bun, a deep red lip, and strong yet minimal silhouettes. As the band is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame this weekend, there’s never been a better time to reflect on the British-Nigerian singer’s personal style. Think: sweaters with strong shoulders, thick belts on long cinched skirts, and, when called for, a perfectly eccentric evening jacket souped up with embroidery and satisfyingly present buttons.

Chalk it up to her era; Sade exploded in popularity in the ’80s, when these kinds of powerful silhouettes reigned supreme, but even beyond that, she knew the power of style. And it’s no wonder: Years ago, in a rare radio interview, she divulged that fashion was her passion long before music. “I made clothes. For three years I went to an art college and did fashion at Central Saint Martins in London,” she said. “I actually sold clothes, and that’s when I started to sing. I had to make a choice between doing the two, because I didn’t have enough time.” Though her foray into design was incredibly sparsely documented, her focus was on menswear, and she later co-founded the tailored menswear fashion label Demob with designer Sarah Lee, where the duo created club-kid-ready attire.

Onstage, whether she was singing “Smooth Operator” or “No Ordinary Love,” she wore her finishing touches with pride: lush little leather gloves in olive green to match a soft-shouldered woolen suit, or a festooning delicate statement necklace layered over a black tank top. Rather than layer multiple pieces, she communicates through the subtle impact of one-and-done statements. A delicate stack of bracelets, or modernist front-facing Lucite hoop earrings, for instance. She usually leans into white and black, except for the rare occasion when she chooses a jammy, rich shade of plum or deep olive green. Her attention to detail does not go unnoticed; there’s a clear knack for tailored silhouettes.

Sade’s elusive nature combined with the ethereal sound of her music also contributes to fashion forming her memorable identity. Long before others made a plain turtleneck or slicked-back hairstyle their uniform, there was Sade doing it authentically, and with accessorized flair. And in today’s era of highly produced musicians who are styled by a team, Sade still stands out.

Though Sade and her band will not be present at the ceremony, they called it “both a gift and a timely reminder to give thanks, not only to those who voted for us but also every single person who lets our music into their lives” in a statement. For every person who’s ever loved an accessory and a bold shoulder look (especially gold hoop earrings), Sade’s presence lives on beyond the music too.
