#6653. The Miami Heat Dropped Brand-New Jerseys Just in Time for Grand Theft Auto VI

Growing up in Oakland, Miami Heat forward Keshad Johnson and his brother Kenny used to sneak away from their parents to play Grand Theft Auto. “It caused some fights between me and him on turns,” Johnson says. “We used to play that if you crash the car, you gotta pass the sticks.”

For many of us who came of age in the early aughts, sneaking away from our parents to play GTA was a rite of passage. And since the first edition of the game dropped in 1997, at least part of the thrill of this fictional world was often tied to the clandestine affair. But next week, Johnson won’t be hiding from anybody. Instead, he’ll be part of a once-in-a-lifetime Grand Theft Auto experience when he and his Heat teammates take the court in special-edition Vice City jerseys inspired by the game.

Grand Theft Auto VI, Vice City, launches on November 19th. But the night before, when the Heat and superstar Giannis Antetokounmpo take on his former team, the Milwaukee Bucks, they'll be ringing in what is by most accounts the biggest video game launch of all time with a special event that only Rockstar Games and the Heat could pull off. “My whole family is trying to get a Vice City jersey,” Johnson said when we spoke last weekend.

“We're bringing sports and entertainment together in a way that's never been done,” adds Miami Heat Chief Creative Officer Jennifer Alvarez. “And we're going to deliver an experience that no one has actually had at an NBA game.”

More on that in a second. But let’s start with the kits: all black, with bright pink accents that pop like neon signs in the South Beach sky. The word “Heat” is splashed across the front. “It's kind of like the outlaw type vibe,” Johnson said. “That's what we want to give when we're on the court.”

Hidden inside the letters and jersey numbers is a map of Miami streets. They were designed by Nike and Travis Scott’s Cactus Jack, whose logos are featured on the jersey and shorts. As the whole campaign makes clear, details matter.

“I feel like Vice City has its own fashion culture,” says Heat star Bam Adebayo.

The jerseys will be available for purchase on game night at the arena, where fans will be transported into the video game itself upon entering the Kaseya Center, whose plaza will be made over with a Grotti Cheetah and Albany Manana, just two of the sports cars one can drive in GTA.

A sign hoisted atop the arena will read “Welcome to Vice City.” In fact, Mitchell was late to practice one day because his usual route was blocked by a helicopter that’d been deployed to help install it. “It shows how much time and effort they're trying to put into this new game,” Mitchell says. “This is probably gonna be the greatest game of all time.”

Though everyone involved has kept tight-lipped about what happens once inside the arena, fans attending Heat games have already been able to order burgers from Burger Shot and chicken from Cluckin' Bell, two fictional fast-food chains in the Grand Theft Auto universe. “It's a full 360 experience. I can't wait for people to really understand what that means,” Alvarez said, coyly. “And that's all I can say about it.”

One can understand the secrecy, since the Heat’s Vice City takeover has been two years in the making. It all started when Rockstar Games dropped the trailer for Vice City in December 2023. A digital Kaseya Center can be seen in the first 30 seconds.

“When we saw that we were in the trailer, we thought we should figure something out,” Alvarez recalls. “Because we've been synonymous with the word Vice since 2017."

The Heat launched the Miami Vice campaign in 2017 with its acclaimed Original Vice jerseys that set the standard for NBA teams launching City Edition jerseys. Those campaigns went beyond the uniforms and included local activations like custom license plates and a fashion line created in collaboration with local artists. Over the years, the Heat launched five separate Vice jerseys, each campaign expanding on previous ones. Ask those with the Heat, and they’d agree that this latest installment is the biggest one yet. “It feels like all of it built up to this,” Alvarez said.

To be clear, the Heat don’t look at this as an extension of their own Vice line. Rather, this is meant to be as exclusive as any streetwear brand launch. Also, it’s not easy to transport fans into a video game every single night. Go big, then go home.

Meanwhile, Rockstar has infiltrated Miami, turning the city that inspired Vice City into Vice City itself. Burger Shot came to life through a collaboration with Skinny Louie, a local smash-burger joint that has rebranded their brick-and-mortar (and arena) locations for the launch. Rockstar Games has activations throughout the city, including in Downtown, Little Haiti and the famous Wynwood Walls. It’s an Inception-style, video game outside the video game-type thing that crescendos with the Heat game on the eve of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch.

Players got their first look at the jerseys and the campaign during a team meeting in early October. After hours of presentations about business operations, media responsibilities and other team matters, the energy in the room sparked when Alvarez took the microphone and showed the first Vice City slide. The players locked in. A few even stood up and cheered.

Mitchell, for his part, was taken back to his childhood, when he would come home from his grandma’s house and play Grand Theft Auto until it was time for bed. For a while, Mitchell became obsessed, playing GTA while other popular games like Call of Duty and NBA 2K collected dust.

“I just played that all the time, doing missions, but also just running around,” he remembers. “It's kind of like your own world in a way.”

And next week, he’ll get to enter it IRL.

#6652. 3 Easy Hacks To Make Instant Mashed Potatoes WAY Better

You might prefer homemade mashed potatoes, but sometimes you just need a shortcut—and on days like that, grabbing the box is WAY easier. But while the back-of-the-box directions will yield just-fine results, a few easy hacks will give you much better results.

As a recipe developer and professional cook, I don’t often make instant mashed potatoes, but I was excited by the challenge of leveling them up—without adding a bunch of extra ingredients or steps that take the convenience out of this convenience food. So I tried making instant mashed potatoes every way I could think of (including the way the box says!). In the end, I found three tricks that, while super simple, massively improve that final bowl of mashed potatoes.

Here are three ways to instantly upgrade instant mashed potatoes.

Most boxes tell you to rehydrate instant mashed potato flakes in hot water enriched with a little butter and a few tablespoons of milk—but I’m going all in on the milk here. The extra dairy really fills out the flavor of the mashed potato and makes it creamier—especially if you’re using a higher-fat milk, like whole or 2%.

When swapping milk for water, it’s best to increase the liquid amount just slightly. For some reason (totally scientific, I’m sure!), the potato flakes require more milk than water to hydrate properly. I recommend 2 extra tablespoons for every half cup of instant mashed potatoes.

Also, add the extra milk the box typically calls for. If you leave it out, the potatoes will be dry. When I was testing, I found it didn’t really matter when that second amount of milk went into the pan (at the beginning versus just before the potatoes), but some boxes emphasize putting it in cold just before adding the potatoes—so if you want to do that to make you feel safer, be my guest!

All the instant mashed potatoes I made lacked seasoning—until I doubled the salt. Then they were perfect. Now here’s the thing: I was testing with Diamond Crystal kosher salt, which is less salty by volume than table salt or Morton’s kosher. The back of the instant mashed potato box didn’t specify what type of salt they used, so if they tested with a fine salt or Morton’s kosher, maybe ¼ teaspoon was the perfect amount. But in my kitchen with Diamond Crystal, it was woefully underseasoned.

Maybe you’re nervous about oversalting and don’t want to double or even slightly increase the salt right away. But regardless, I’m begging you: Taste those potatoes before you serve them and don’t feel bad if you have to add another hefty pinch.

You might assume that mashed potatoes should be made in a pot—I definitely did. But the fluffiest, creamiest instant potatoes I made in this whole testing process came from a wide, high-sided sauté pan. The reason for this? Absolute science.

When adding the instant potato flakes to the hot liquid, the goal is to distribute them as evenly as possible without working them too much. Yes, the back of the box says to “stir” the potatoes in, but in testing, I quickly discovered that even a few strokes can quickly lead to gummy potatoes.

Here’s where the pan size comes in. Using a wide pan increases the liquid's surface area, so you can sprinkle the potatoes evenly over the top and pat them down into the liquid instead of stirring. From there, let them stand until they’ve absorbed the liquid, then give them a few stirs. Trust me: They’ll be way fluffier because you messed with them less!

#6650. The 11 Best Makeup Brush Sets, According to Experts

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

If you’re reading this, it’s probably time for a new set

Crafting the perfect smoky eye or no-makeup-makeup finish isn’t always easy, no matter how many TikTok tutorials you’ve watched. But beyond having the skills to pull off a glamorous beauty look, using one of the best makeup brush sets can make all the difference in your concealer placement, blush intensity, and more.

Even the most talented artists need the right tools to get the best results, which is why we’ve consulted professionals like Anisa Telwar Kaicker, founder of Anisa Beauty, and professional makeup artist and master esthetician Nicole Erickson for their top picks.

Whether you’re a budding professional, a total beginner, or just looking to upgrade your beauty routine, we’ve included some of the best makeup brush sets below that might actually make you want to clean your tools after each use. Plus, experts share tips on choosing the best makeup brush set for your skill level and preferred makeup looks, and weigh in on the natural-versus-synthetic bristle debate.

Celebrity makeup artist and Makeup by Mario founder Mario Dedivanovic just dropped this trio of dual-ended face and eye brushes, and Bazaar editors couldn’t be more excited to put them to use. The limited edition bundle is highly versatile, and nicely includes a carrying pouch for easy transport.

Type of brushes included: F3 dual-ended Precision Powder brush, F4 dual-ended Foundation and Face brush, E6 dual-ended Eyeshadow brush

New to makeup application? This five-piece brush set from makeup artist Laura Geller is designed to streamline your routine, not complicate it. The standout is the retractable kabuki brush, which buffs powder, cream, or liquid foundation for a diffused, airbrushed look. Plus, its retractable design helps minimize messes in your makeup bag. The set also includes two eyeshadow brushes—one for all-over color and another for creating smoky eyes—an angled brush for blush and bronzer, and a large, fluffy brush for adding a soft, bronzed glow to the high points of your face.

Type of brushes included: Retractable kabuki brush, angled blush brush, face brush, all-over eyeshadow brush, blending crease brush

Dirty makeup brushes can harbor breakout-causing bacteria, so Morphe upgraded its popular makeup brush sets with antibacterial synthetic bristles. While you’ll still need to wash your tools regularly, the silver-ion-infused material will put your mind at ease during day-to-day use. Suitable for beginners and experts alike, this eight-piece kit is a great choice for anyone looking for a fresh start.

Brushes included: M104 Domed foundation brush, M133 domed concealer brush, M161 large rounded powder brush, M204 rounded blush brush, M303 large paddle packer eyeshadow brush, M332 medium rounded blender eyeshadow brush, M383 pointed detail eye brush, M401 dual-ended angled brow brush and spoolie

If you’re after the essentials, grab this six-piece Real Techniques set for just $20. More than 40,000 five-star Amazon reviewers say these budget-friendly brushes are versatile enough for most everyday makeup looks and durable enough to withstand years of daily use.

“You don’t necessarily need to buy the most expensive set on the market,” Erickson notes. “Affordable makeup brush brands like Real Techniques and Eco Tools are sufficient for those wanting to keep it simple. Assess what you’re doing makeup-wise daily and consider what you actually need.”

Number of brushes: Four (plus two makeup sponges)

Types of brushes included: RT 400 blush brush, RT 300 deluxe crease brush, RT 402 setting brush, RT 200 expert face brush

Another great option for beginners, this budget-friendly set includes the basic face and eye brushes you need to apply go-to products like concealer, blush, and eyeshadow—without overwhelming you with options for blending and detailing.

Erickson also points out that many beauty products don’t require brushes at all. “If you’re a minimalist, there are quite a few cream-based face products and even eyeshadows you can apply with your fingers. Using your fingers can also help to warm up and blend the product—just make sure your hands are clean.”

Brushes included: Full face blush brush, angled foundation face brush, blurring concealer brush, defined crease eye brush, angled liner eye brush

If you’re the type to do your makeup in the gym locker room or during your morning commute, try this travel-friendly brush set from Hourglass Cosmetics. This seven-piece assortment includes cult-favorite tools you’ve likely seen on TikTok, including the brand’s dual-ended Ambient Lighting Edit Brush, all housed in a luxe vegan leather roll.

Types of brushes included: Vanish seamless finish foundation brush, vanish seamless finish concealer brush, veil single powder brush, ambient lighting edit brush, N° 6 tapered blender brush, N° 12 beveled shadow brush, N° 14 detail setting brush

If you’re a fan of Saie’s makeup essentials, we bet you’ll love applying them with this brand’s six-piece brush set. Three brushes in varying sizes and textures help you create a natural-looking base with your preferred liquid, cream, and powder complexion products. Then, you can go in with the dual-ended brush for highlighter, concealer or bronzer, add a rosy flush with the powder blush brush, and finish with your favorite setting powder using the all-over powder brush.

Brushes included: Base brush, fluffy brush, big brush, double brush

Thoughtfully designed ergonomic handles make these Guide Beauty brushes a great choice for everyone, including makeup lovers with limited mobility. Rest the brand’s signature Guide Ring between your fingers and place your thumb on the pad for a comfortable grip that gives you total control, even if you struggle with shaky hands.

Brushes included: All-over eyeshadow brush, blend & crease brush, define & smudge brush

If your current face makeup brushes aren’t cutting it, upgrade to this do-it-all duo from Anisa Beauty. The larger brush, the brand’s cult-favorite Pinnacle Foundation Brush, features angled bristles that curve to your face contours, blending liquid foundation, cream blush, and bronzer effortlessly. The compact concealer brush fits perfectly under the eyes for a smooth, crease-free finish.

“This set of brushes from Anisa Beauty makes applying my base makeup a dream,” beauty commerce editor Tiffany Dodson Davis says. “Not only are the bristles super soft, but their angled shapes make it easy to blend my foundation and concealer quickly and seamlessly.”

Brushes included: Pinnacle foundation brush, angled concealer brush

What Are the Best Makeup Brushes Worth Shopping?

According to Erickson, the most essential makeup brushes in your set are the ones you use with powder products, such as bronzer, blush, or setting powder. "Everyone should own a small powder brush—or even something that resembles a large eyeshadow brush—to cut shine where needed and set concealer. An angled brush can be helpful when using bronzer or contour, as well as a medium-sized cheek brush for powder blush."

And when it comes to eye makeup brushes, the expert adds, "It can be helpful to have a dual-sided angled brush-spoolie combo for brows, as well as for winged liner. A small, dense, pointed brush for the lash line and inner corner is nice to have, as well as one or two blending brushes for the eyelids."

Should I Opt for Synthetic or Natural Bristles?

"I like to say there is nothing 'natural' about animal hair," Anisa Telwar Kaicker tells Bazaar. "It can dry faster and break more quickly. Man-made synthetics can be long-lasting, hygienic, innovative in shape, and soft to the touch."

Erickson agrees that synthetic makeup brushes outperform products made using animal by-products. "Synthetic brushes tend to be more durable and last longer. Less and less natural bristles areused today, and as a makeup artist, I don’t think we need them, performance-wise."

What’s the Most Effective Way to Clean Makeup Brushes?

"When I deep clean my makeup brushes once or twice a month, I typically use Dr. Bronner’s 18-in-1 castile soap," Erickson notes. "At the very least, use a quick-dry brush cleaner like Sephora’s Daily Brush Cleaner between each use to avoid the spread of bacteria."

Telwar Kaicker suggests that after deep cleaning, you remove excess water from your brushes with a towel. Then, tilt the brush downward to prevent water from seeping into the ferrule and breaking down the glue in the brush head.

How Often Should I Replace My Makeup Brushes?

According to Erickson, high-quality, well-cared-for brushes can last for years. "If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. I’ve had some of my makeup brushes last a decade and some only last a year or two. If you love it and you’re able to properly sanitize it, use it for as long as you can."

How do you know when it's time for a new set? Erickson says it all comes down to the glue. "Typically, when a makeup brush goes bad, the glue between the brush and handle starts to break down due to wear and moisture from cleaning. When that happens, toss it and move on. For beauty blenders and sponges that harbor bacteria, toss them after a few uses, no matter how well you sanitize them. Toss after a few uses, especially if you’re acne-prone."

#6649. I Own 400 Sneakers. You Should Only Own 21

I own far too many sneakers. There are everyday beaters, rare samples, and plenty in between, accumulated over more than a decade of collecting. That’s a lot of shoes by any reasonable measure. Around 400 at my last count. A few of my favorites took some work to get. I entered a stupid number of raffles for the JJJJound x New Balance 990v3, lined up overnight for the Sacai x Nike VaporWaffle, and caved and paid resale for the Gucci x Adidas Gazelle.

With that many pairs, you start thinking about what actually earns its space. A shoe can be interesting to collect and difficult to wear. Another can seem almost too obvious to buy, then turn out to be the thing that works with most of your clothes. If I could wipe the slate clean, I’d pay much more attention to that second category. I’d still want some fun stuff, obviously. I’m rebuilding a sneaker collection, not writing a packing list.

So, where would I start? With these 21 pairs from Foot Locker’s selection. There are basketball shoes I’d want for their shape and history, runners I’d buy for everyday wear, and a few low-profile pairs to switch things up. Some are famous enough that they barely need an introduction. But knowing a shoe’s name and knowing why you’d want it in your collection are different things. Here’s why these would make it back into mine.

Yes, four of my first five picks are Nike or Jordan – and that’s deliberate. If I were rebuilding my collection, they’d still get a big chunk of my budget. The Air Jordan 1, Air Force 1, and Dunk are a pretty good explanation for why. If you’re starting with jeans and a tee, I’d look here first. A high-top gives you a little more shoe around the ankle. A low-top is easier with shorts, and white Forces can do a lot of the work when you’re getting dressed in a hurry.

I’d start right here, before getting distracted by anything limited to 200 pairs. Peter Moore’s 1985 design gets the shape so right: the height of the collar, the panels around the toe, the way contrasting colors divide up the upper. The High OG also gives you the Nike Air tongue branding. I want a pair that looks good with straightforward jeans and a tee, and the Air Jordan 1 has been perfecting that combo for decades.

A fresh white Air Force 1 would be an early purchase for the deeply boring reason that I’d wear it constantly. Bruce Kilgore’s 1982 basketball silhouette has enough weight to sit properly under loose jeans, and that beefy sole gives the whole fit a little more presence. White-on-white also makes the leather panels and perforations easier to appreciate. It’s the pair I’d reach for when I like everything else I’m wearing and don’t need to complicate things.

Once you’ve looked at enough Dunks, you notice how much the colorblocking changes the sneaker. Its college basketball background gave those panels a specific purpose: carrying team colors. The ‘Sanded Purple’ makes good use of that layout. I’d want a Dunk Low because the shape is uncomplicated enough to wear regularly, while the colors give an outfit a clear starting point. Pick up one of those shades elsewhere, or leave the rest nice and neutral.

The Superstar arrived as a basketball shoe in 1970; Run-D.M.C.’s “My Adidas” helped give it a very different audience in 1986. That history is good to know, but the Shelltoe is what would get my money. It gives the front of the shoe a distinctive shape, and the Superstar II’s extra padding makes the whole thing feel chunkier than the OG. I’d put these under straight jeans, with enough of the toe showing to appreciate it.

The High would come first, of course, but I’d still make room for an Air Jordan 1 Low OG. Removing the tall collar changes how the panels sit with your pants, giving you more space around the ankle and a less bulky-looking sneaker. I’d buy it for days when I want that familiar Jordan colorblocking with shorts or slightly shorter pants. There’s enough difference to justify the second box.

For a day with a lot of walking, I’d start with the 990v6 or the Zoom Vomero 5. There are plenty of ways to get that mesh running-shoe look, and the XT-6 is the one I’d pick if I wanted a trail sole with more grip.

Yes, there would absolutely be gray New Balances in the rebuild. The 990 family started in 1982, but the sixth-gen adds FuelCell cushioning and lets the suede overlays flow across the mesh without the usual midfoot saddle. You can see the difference, and there’s a practical benefit underfoot, too. This is the pair I’d buy for days with a lot of walking: comfy enough to justify the purchase, good-looking enough that comfort isn’t the only justification.

The OG 2008 Gel-Kayano 14 was the first in the series designed by someone other than Toshikazu Kayano – useful information for your next deeply specific sneaker convo. More relevant here is how well the layered mesh and synthetic overlays work together. The ‘Graphite Grey’ has enough contrast to show off the construction, with Gel cushioning right underneath.

The 1906R is for when I want all the little technical details. Open mesh, curvy overlays, and segmented cushioning around the heel give you plenty to check out, especially in white, silver, and black. It shares the same sole tech with the 2002R and 860v2, but the upper just looks more put-together.

The Zoom Vomero 5 launched back in 2011, but it didn’t gain its cult following until about a decade later. There’s a lot to enjoy up top: open mesh, overlapping panels, and plastic caging that becomes particularly obvious in ‘Metallic Silver’. Zoom Air cushioning gives it a practical role in the collection, too. I’d buy this as a regular-wear pair for long days, with enough detail to make jeans and a plain sweater look put together.

First released in 2010, the Omni 9 has all the mesh and supporting structure you’d expect from a running shoe of that era. This white and pink version lets you see how the layers fit together, with ProGrid cushioning underneath. I’d want it because a collection can become very repetitive once you find a couple of brands you like. The Omni gives me another interpretation of the technical runner, with enough character to earn its place alongside the Nikes and Asics.

The P-6000 looks like a straight archive reissue, but it actually combines elements from the Pegasus 25 and Pegasus 2006. I’d buy the white and silver combo and wear the hell out of them – every pair doesn’t need to be an occasion.

The XT-6 started life in 2013 as a serious trail running shoe, and you can still see that purpose in the reinforced upper, Quicklace system, and lugged outsole. My plans would probably involve considerably less altitude. I’d buy it because the close-fitting upper and outdoor construction bring something different to the collection, particularly with cargo pants or wider-leg pants. The ‘Black Coffee’ also makes it easy to wear with denim, olive, and navy. No hiking itinerary required.

If your jeans taper or you like a shorter hem, try something that sits closer to the foot. The Samba is an easy place to start in black leather. I’d go for the green Spezial if I wanted a little color without having to think too hard about the rest of the fit.

Collecting can make you weird about buying something that everybody else owns – I’d try to avoid that with the Samba. Its roots go back to soccer shoes for icy fields in 1950, but the slim shape is what earns it a place here. After a few chunky basketball shoes, you need something that sits closer to the foot. ‘Core Black’ leather, white stripes, and a suede T-toe give you plenty to work with, particularly under a straighter pair of pants.

Yes, there’s already a Samba here. The Handball Spezial earns its own place with its rounded toe, suede upper, and gum sole, which give it a softer appearance than the leather-heavy pairs. First made for handball players in 1979, it’s also a good way to bring some color into the rebuild. The green and white do enough on their own. I’d wear these with blue jeans and let the suede take care of the rest.

The Gazelle dates back to 1966, making this year its 60th birthday. I’d buy it for the suede upper and the straightforward proportions, which give it a slightly different feel from the other Adidas silhouettes here. In black and white, it’s easy to wear with faded denim or dark pants. Some days, a familiar shape in simple colors is exactly what you want.

Puma’s Suede history runs back to 1968, so I’d want some of that history in the collection, as well as the shoe’s simple construction. The soft upper and sweeping Formstrip give you texture and shape without a bunch of extra panels. It would be a useful change after several technical runners, especially with denim or cotton pants that already have plenty of texture themselves.

Wide jeans and heavier layers can take a bigger shoe. I’d look at the Air Max 95 for the layered upper, the Gel-NYC if I wanted something a little quieter, or the 9060 if I wanted the sole to do most of the talking.

Sergio Lozano was inspired by human anatomy for the Air Max 95, translating ribs, muscle fibers, and a spine into a running shoe. A pretty weird design concept that produced a very good sneaker. Those layered side panels are the reason I’d buy it again: they give the shoe depth even in this low-key black, white, and gray combination. It has enough bulk for wider pants, and enough going on that the rest of the fit can stay simple.

The Gel-NYC looks pretty old school, but Asics actually assembled it from several archive references. There’s Gel-Nimbus 3 and Gel-MC Plus V in the upper, with Gel-Cumulus 16 tooling underneath. The result has a fuller shape than the Kayano, with more emphasis on those broad suede panels. That’s why I’d make room for both. This ‘Cream’ and ‘Oyster Grey’ version works particularly well beneath wider pants, where a very slim shoe can disappear under the hem.

A collection of completely sensible sneakers would feel like an opportunity missed. The 9060 takes details from New Balance’s 99X family and blows them up: the 990’s sway bars spread across the upper, while the sole gets a sculpted, pod-like shape. I’d pick this brown version to balance out bigger pants and heavier layers. It gives those clothes a chunky enough shoe to sit over.

These are the two I’d happily get dirty. Go for the Chucks if you like a high-top with cuffed jeans, or the Old Skools if you want something low that’s just as easy to wear with shorts.

Black canvas Chucks would be back on the shelf pretty quickly, too. Their basketball DNA stretches all the way back to 1917, but it’s the narrow shape I’d want in this collection. It gives jeans a completely different finish from an AF1 or a 990, especially with a little ankle showing. These are also shoes I’d be happy to wear until the canvas softened and the rubber picked up some marks.

To finish off my new collection, I’d grab a pair of Old Skools. Launched in 1977 as the Style 36, it introduced the Jazz Stripe along the way. The canvas-and-suede upper, white stripe, and waffle sole are still enough to make it worth owning. It looks good with jeans, works with shorts, and improves once the upper loosens up. After all the comparing and researching and rebuilding, I’d want at least one pair I could put on and forget about.

#6647. Cranberry Pie

What People Are Saying:“I made 3 desserts this Thanksgiving and this was an absolute hit!! Everyone at the table raved about it including my super picky 7 year old who had herself seconds. Definitely a winner and will be making again.” - PurplePuzzle

Preheat your oven to 350° and grease a 9-inch pie plate with butter.

For the crust, grab a large bowl and mix together the Biscoff crumbs, melted butter, and a pinch of salt. Gently press this mixture into the bottom and up the sides of your greased pie plate.

Bake the crust until it turns golden and feels firm to the touch. Once done, set it aside on a wire rack to cool.

In a small bowl, mix the gelatin with some cold water and let it sit so it can bloom.

Next, for the filling, grab a medium saucepan, toss in the cranberries, brown sugar, orange juice, and zest, and bring it to a simmer over medium heat. Stir occasionally while the cranberries burst and the liquid has thickened slightly, which should take about 7 minutes.

Pour in the coconut milk, ginger, heavy cream, almond extract, and a little salt. Stir everything together and heat until it’s nice and steamy, but not quite simmering. Remove from the heat and stir in the bloomed gelatin until fully dissolved.

Now, blend the cranberry mixture until it’s super smooth—use whatever blender or food processor you have handy. Strain it into a bowl, toss out any solids, and let the mixture cool down to room temperature. Pour the cranberry filling into your crust and refrigerate until set, which should take at least 6 hours.

Serve with homemade whipped cream and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

This pie will keep for up to a week in the fridge and frozen for up to 5 months. Simply thaw it out in the fridge the next day and serve.

#6645. Read Dodie Kazanjian’s In-Depth 1994 Richard Avedon Profile for Vogue

“Avedon’s Eye,” by Dodie Kazanjian, was originally published in the February 1994 issue of Vogue.

For more of the best from Vogue’s archive, sign up for our Nostalgia newsletter here.

Richard Avedon made four trips to Stockholm a few years ago to see Ingmar Bergman’s production of Long Day’s Journey into Night, in Swedish. He saw it seven times. “There’s no movie I could see seven times, but when a great living performance captures me, I could go every night, forever . . . . At the Royal Dramatic Theater in Stockholm, when you go upstairs for coffee during intermission, there’s a place on the ceiling where they have the masks of comedy and tragedy—and they’re both tragedy! Because you’re in Sweden. So it’s the perfect place for me, obviously.”

There’s some irony here but also a valid point. Theater is the guiding metaphor in Richard Avedon’s life, as well as his work. An element of drama gets into everything he does, and the last few months have certainly brought him center stage. The most famous American photographer of our time has been up to his ears in publicity (and controversy) over his recently published book of photographs—which he calls An Autobiography—and over the major retrospective of his work that opens on March 24 at the Whitney Museum. Attention is being paid: 30 pages in Newsweek on the man and his work; appearances on Prime-Time Live, the Today show, and Charlie Rose; a black-tie gala at the New York Public Library for 300 people, thrown by husband-and-wife team Harold Evans, head of Random House (which published An Autobiography), and Tina Brown, The New Yorker’s editor, who a year ago made Avedon the magazine’s first and only staff photographer. At the age of 70, Avedon has shifted his half-century career into overdrive, but somehow he still manages to find time to make dinner arrangements with this reporter for a gourmet meal that he cooks himself.

In a manner of speaking, that is. “You call this cooking?” Dick scoffs, in his unmistakable rasp—New York accented but with other ingredients, mostly untraceable. “I’m an executive cook,” he says. Verlie Fisher, his longtime housekeeper, made the herbed chicken that afternoon and left foolproof instructions for heating it up. We are in the kitchen and dining area of his loft, a vast and monumentally cluttered space on the second floor of an Upper East Side town house that was once a commercial laundry. The legendary Avedon studio is downstairs, the main part of it anyway; additional workspaces for his team of fifteen associates have taken root on the two floors above his living quarters. Your first impression here is that there’s too much of everything. There are seventeen different-size lighted candles on the long dining table, and bowls of blueberries and blackberries and nuts and cheeses, and photographs both framed and unframed, and pots of narcissus and orchids, and an out-of-control bamboo tree that brushes the ceiling, and a bright red leather boxing glove that’s just arrived from Paris. (“Since this was a rough week for me, a French friend sent it over.”)

Avedon is in constant motion, checking the oven, darting here and there, running his fingers through his long silver-white hair, reaching under his glasses to rub his eyes. A lithe, compact bundle of nervous energy, he is wearing blue jeans, loafers without socks, and a blue shirt with ASTAIRE LIVES printed on the pocket; he had it put there because this was the shirt he was wearing when he heard that Fred Astaire, his childhood idol, had just died. With Avedon, conversation doesn’t just flow—it runs and jumps and turns on a dime and sometimes goes in two or more directions at once. In the fifteen minutes before dinner is ready, he covers the origins of his three favorite chicken recipes (Janet Cam’s Buddhist Chicken, Marcella Hazan’s Chicken with Three Lemons, and Verlie’s own Herbed Chicken); Chekhov’s short stories— “Did you know that he wrote 300? I’ve ordered the whole thirteen-volume set”; his son John’s work as a foreign relations adviser to and biographer of the Dalai Lama of Tibet; the young boxer in Phoenix, whom he photographed for The New Yorker yesterday; the three negative reviews of An Autobiography in The New York Times, which should have killed sales of the $100 book but didn’t; and the critical knives that are being whetted for his Whitney show, which was viciously attacked by Hilton Kramer in The New York Observer two years in advance of its opening. (“This is the ultimate capitulation to celebrity, money and fashion at the expense of art.”) “Reviews no longer victimize me,” Avedon says. “Or define me, or elate me, or stop me from working.”

In The New York Times Book Review, Maud Lavin wrote, “Mr. Avedon’s close, hard stare, his emptied backgrounds and his graphically spectacular compositions do not tell us any more about the social context of napalm victims than they do about fashion models. These techniques do not unmask the ambiguities of people’s lives. What they demonstrate is the extraordinary high degree of control Mr. Avedon exerts in all his confrontations with his subjects.” In the daily Times, Margo Jefferson said of the portraits in Avedon’s book, “By the end, I was rooting for anyone who managed to escape with a shred of self-determination intact.” Andy Grundberg’s more recent notice in the Book Review said that An Autobiography showed Avedon “at his most characteristic: controlling of his subjects and manipulative of his audience, driven to redeem himself from the taint of commerce, obsessed with the judgments of a disembodied posterity.”

Why does Avedon get attacked so savagely? His tremendous success as a fashion photographer is one obvious reason: How dare he presume to be an artist as well? Avedon has fought this dichotomy all his professional life, insisting that there is no difference between his fashion work, his reportage, and the body of portraiture that is his principal claim to recognition as an artist. “I think art history will see him as one of the great portraitists of the twentieth century,” says David Ross, the Whitney’s director, who has come in for a lot of abuse himself over his decision to present an Avedon retrospective. “He’s spent so much of his life in analysis, and in the quest of understanding who he is—this tortured, self-driven Jewish man who is trying to understand himself by looking at other people and their lives, and looking at the way things work, and trying to see into that borderline area between madness and beauty and power and powerlessness. He’s looked hard, as all great artists do.”

Ross insists that working with Avedon on the Whitney retrospective did not involve pitched battles over who was in control. “When we started working on this show, I said to Dick, ‘This is the show that needs to be done for you, not by you; you need to have that happen, as every artist does.’ On the design level, Dick was as directorial as ever. You would have to be a complete fool not to make use of Dick and Mary Shanahan, an amazing designer who works with him. But on a curatorial level, he really let Jane Livingston choose the show. The primary selection of pictures, the primary story that’s being told in the show and in the catalog, is Jane’s.”

The oven timer announces that the chicken is ready. He carves it deftly, serves it with his special house salad—tiny mâche lettuce leaves and shaved Parmesan. The bread is folded into the napkins to keep it fresh. The wine is a 1987 Margaux. The plates are oversize Italian faience from Siena, boldly colorful against the deep blue tablecloth. “You mustn’t think that I care about candle colors and tablecloths and stuff like that,” he says. He does care, nevertheless. It’s all part of the Avedon performance, a never-ending engagement with the visual world in all its forms.

Is it unfair to say that Avedon’s portraits are manipulative, overly controlled, and “trapped in narcissism,” as Maud Lavin charged in The New York Times? This criticism is often heard, and to some extent it may be justified. But then, all great portraits are in a sense self-portraits, and all artists exercise manipulation and control. When Avedon takes a portrait, it is the record of an intense, indelibly personal encounter between the photographer and the subject, whether the subject happens to be a fashion model or a drifter, an actor or a napalm victim, ex-president Dwight David Eisenhower or Jacob Israel Avedon, the photographer’s 87-year-old father, dying of cancer. And if there is sometimes more of Richard Avedon than of the subject in this encounter, well, that’s all in the nature of the performance that Avedon demands in his life and work. But what if the subject won’t perform? Doesn’t this happen in his current avatar as The New Yorker’s staff photographer? “Oh, yes,” he says. “Of course. I’m about as interested in David Dinkins and Rudy Giuliani . . . but that’s part of the job. I’m quite willing to do photographs that are not pure expressions of myself, like the one of Steve Martin on the wall here. He was enormously generous in the sitting, but there’s no such thing as cutting through to Steve Martin. Steve Martin uses his comic genius like a wall. There’s no penetrating it, and I respect that.” Later, he shows me the note Steve Martin sent him after the sitting: "Dear Richard, Yours was the first photo shoot I ever enjoyed . . . . I hope we can become very close friends forsaking all others and have lunches and dinners together six days a week.”

David Ross told me a story about watching Avedon at work on his photographic series called In the American West. “One of the great emblematic West pictures is of a guy with his shirt half over his shoulders. He has a kind of S-shaped body. I remember seeing that guy on the midway of a state fair in southern Colorado. He was the kind of guy I would have crossed the street to avoid. He was tough, and angry, and on the line of being psychotic, and all my good Jewish radar tells me stay away, no eye contact, keep moving. But Dick goes right up and starts talking to him, and within five minutes he is pouring his energy out for Dick in front of a white drop cloth tacked up on a side of a shed. It was astounding to see how he communicates and puts people at ease and allows them to come through.”

Dick is slightly displeased with himself over the chicken. “A little dry, don’t you think? It’s so nice when it’s really juicy. I think we didn’t need that last fifteen minutes.” He has another helping anyway. And he orders me to strip my wishbone clean so he can hang it on the lip of a special pitcher that holds ten or twelve others. “I still have wishes,” he says. “Being 70 doesn’t preclude that.” Dinner consists of one main course plus dessert, simple but extravagant. Another time, you might have a baked potato smothered in beluga caviar, or the special borscht that he carried home in a cardboard container one night from a Russian restaurant in Brighton Beach—he enriches it with piroshki. If he’s serving pasta, it will be Cipriani’s, or else mushroom pasta by his friend China Machado, who was once one of his models and now has a store in Water Mill. Long Island. He jumps up and brings over a box of the Cipriani pasta from the open larder shelves on which are stacked sixteen others. “Just try one of these,” he says of the Cipriani masterpiece. “It takes about a minute and a half to cook. It’s all egg.”

A few days earlier, he had told me that I didn’t have an “Avedon face.” I ask him what he means by an Avedon face. “It’s very varied,” he says. “One of the great Avedon faces is Michelangelo Antonioni’s. There are artists just as complicated as Antonioni, but their complexity isn’t available to my camera. Fellini’s was not an Avedon face. Roy Lichtenstein’s is. I can’t explain it exactly. It’s not about being ravaged or flawed. It’s about contradictions, dialogue, arguments. The soul’s confusion on the face.”

Even in his fashion work he captured that confusion, as Penelope Tree attested in a letter to Avedon about her portrait in An Autobiography. “Of course I identified with being caged, isolated, and utterly bewildered, but I thought I was doing a better job of hiding it! Trust you to see right through. I guess you always did.”

The encounter between Avedon and subject is what makes the portrait, and that usually has a lot to do with what Avedon is feeling at the moment he takes the photograph. Does this make him a monster egoist, as some of his critics maintain? Or is he simply doing what Titian, Velázquez, Francis Bacon, or any great artist does? “Of course, of course,” he says. “Art isn’t art because someone uses a paintbrush. Photography is either good or bad, and when it’s good it’s like any art that’s good. It becomes Art.

“What the subject brings to the camera and what I do with that is what makes the photograph. In photographing my father,” he says, referring to the famous series of his father dying, “I was looking at him. and he was looking at me. The last thing he saw as he was dying was his son. It’s clear to me that he became, in that moment, in that image, what he saw. And what he saw was me.”

Avedon had his own portrait taken for this article. He chose the photographer: his great contemporary and rival, Irving Penn. On the day of the sitting. Avedon had the flu and such severe stomach pains that he called his doctor, from Penn’s studio, for a prescription. “Will I be loopy if I take it?” he asked. “I have an interview with the London Times right after this, and then I’m flying to Hyannis Port to photograph Ethel Kennedy.” “No loopier than usual” was the doctor’s reply. Avedon had brought along a legendary coat from the fifties to be photographed in, a heavy old shearling that he had won in a bet with the model Suzy Parker; it had once warmed Marilyn Monroe, and Isabelle Adjani had worn it in an Avedon photograph. Penn took some shots of him in the coat, but the image that won out shows him in an open-collared work shirt, looking haunted and strangely romantic. “He has a drama that we got that I don’t associate with him,” Penn said afterward. “Like something out of the French Revolution.”

Although Avedon had been photographed twice before by Penn, he tells me that this was the first time he had felt “ready” for the experience. “It’s a wonderful picture,” he says, “the only real portrait of me by Penn. Maybe by anybody. He’s caught something. The real strength of any portrait is to go beneath the surface and into the contradictions within the life. And he’s done that so completely in this portrait. It’s about a kind of crumbling part of me that’s a cross between arrogance and suspicion. Penn’s portrait has nothing to do with looking good, and in this case, it has very little to do with composition. It has a rawness—I mean, it’s more of an Avedon than a Penn. Ha! And yet it could never have been taken by anyone but Penn.”

What is the difference between an Avedon portrait and a Penn portrait?

“I think Penn’s great strength lies in his power of composition and in the very still moment that reveals. From the beginning, I’ve felt that any composition that is visible in my photographs takes you away from the direct confrontation that I look for. If anyone said of a picture of mine. ‘Look at the composition in that,’ I’d be embarrassed. I’d know that I failed.

“Rivalry is a funny word to use about Penn and me. It doesn’t cover or even hint at the relationship. In the years when I was at Harper’s Bazaar [ 1945 to 1965] and he was at Vogue, and we were both covering the same celebrities, I watched every move he made, and I think in some way it helped define me. I was always excited by Penn, in awe of Penn, and wanted to top him or equal him, or be the opposite of him. I think of him as a classicist and of me as an eclectic. I was fired by him. inspired by him. pushed by his standards, his rigor, his excellence.”

I ask him which other photographers he has admired. “Certainly Diane Arbus, Julia Margaret Cameron in the old days. But Cartier-Bresson rules. Walker Evans is a miniaturist compared to him. There are wonderful photographers—Robert Frank, for example—who have mastered small areas of the territory Cartier-Bresson laid out. The world of photojournalism is littered with Bresson babies. He is the photographic Tolstoy of the twentieth century.

“Helmut Newton redefined what a fashion photograph could be. He’s the leader of the post-Avedon, post-Penn period. He released everything. He changed what a fashion model could look like and played with vulgarity in a really witty way. After Helmut Newton, you can’t do a certain kind of picture anymore.”

“It’s done all the time, and it’s boring! But when Helmut does it, the erotic focus shifts from the ankle and the smile to the inner thigh.”

It’s a little odd to hear Richard Avedor speak of the post-Avedon, post-Penn period. Bruce Weber, one of today’s top fashion photographers who photographed Avedon for this article, sees his influence as being very much alive and in the present. “Richard Avedon is like this wonderful kid you meet at school, who has more energy than anybody else,” Weber says. “He really is open, he engages you in what’s going on in his life, and he makes you then think about your own. He’s influenced a whole generation of photographers who are working now, me included, in that just simply and purely you want to take photographs and to photograph your own life at the same time. Dick’s work is not about fame. It’s really about still being a kid and not being afraid to shoe it.”

We’re heavily into dessert by this time. Dick always serves at least five—three different ice and an orange cake from Sant Ambroeus, fresh blackberries and raspberries, macaroons from Bonté, and a split of the Billecart-Salmon champagne that he discovered years ago at Chez Panisse. He promises next time to make Mike Nichols’s Peach Orgasm (six fresh peaches, two bananas, one and a half cups of sugar, two cups of sour cream, and the juice of one lemon: blend in blender, then put in ice cream maker). He has a file of recipes that he’s picked up from restaurants and friends in various parts of the world. It’s more than enough for a book, but it will have to wait until he’s finished the ten books he’s already under contract to do for Random House: several more collections of his photographs: four teaching books based on his master classes in fashion photography, reportage, portraiture, and the snapshot; and an autobiographical novel that he says he’ll be working on for the rest of his life.

There’s another kind of autobiography on the walls. Hundreds of photographs, clippings, postcards, notes, mementos, and reproductions of famous paintings are pinned to the soft beaverboard, some of them yellow with age. Shots of Fred Astaire dancing, and one of Astaire with the young Avedon during the filming of Funny Face, in which the great dancer played the part of a fashion photographer based on Richard Avedon. A more mature Avedon with Audrey Hepburn, Miss Funny Face herself. The New York Post’s front page on Liz Taylor’s eighth marriage, with eight “I Do’s” in bold type. Three Avedon press cards for the year he went to Vietnam. A news photo of an unidentified man frozen to death beneath the ice of a lake in Queens, New York. Athletes in violent action. Snapshots of Evelyn, his wife, whom he hasn’t lived with for many years (he still sees her for dinner or a movie at least once a week), and one of their son, John, and John’s wife, Maura Moynihan, the senator’s daughter, with their son, Michael. A blown-up page of The New York Times Magazine with head shots of seventeen people whom Stalin had killed. (“They were photographed and then they were killed,” Avedon says. “Look, aren’t these the most pure and perfect portraits?”) A life-size blowup of Ruby Holden, the Nevada pawnbroker whom Avedon photographed in 1980. A poster of Goya’s Contessa Chinchón, which he considers one of the great portraits in Western art—”an infantile woman in an evening gown,” he says. “A combination of fashion and portraiture. Most portraiture involves fashion. That’s what Penn does. That’s what I try to do.”

Fashion photographs, by Avedon or anyone else, are nonetheless conspicuously absent from this wall of memories and momentary enthusiasms. No Dovima with elephants, no Suzy Parker, no Twiggy, no Jean Shrimpton or Stephanie Seymour, his current favorite. Other than a few isolated examples, only one room (out of fifteen) at the Whitney retrospective will be devoted to Avedon’s fashion work, and this makes you wonder about his reiterated argument that all his work, fashion included, is a part of the same seamless web. Avedon’s ambivalent relationship with the world of high fashion, which has given him the means to pursue his ambitions as an artist, was exacerbated in 1988 when he had a falling out with Vogue’s new editor. He had photographed almost every Vogue cover since 1966 but found he disagreed with Anna Wintour about how Vogue covers should look, and she stopped using him for covers. Recently, on the occasion of this interview, he wrote Wintour a letter and signed it “Let’s bury the lipsticks. Dick.” In the meanwhile, he has not lacked for commercial outlets. Tomorrow he starts a big job for Versace—racks of dresses and underwear and tables of accessories have taken over the far end of the long room, for a weeklong shoot that will be the firm’s next major ad campaign.

The problem is he won’t be using Stephanie Seymour, who is pregnant. “I’ll never forgive her,” he says, mock-seriously. Avedon has always liked to work more or less exclusively with one model at a time. Suzy Parker, his favorite of the fifties, has vivid memories of their working relationship. “We had become so attuned to each other,” she tells me. “First of all, we shared an outrageous sense of humor. Second, we worked to music, so we were already into movement. I mean, I was never still. Before Dick, modeling was like being crucified most of the time. They’d have tissue paper stuffed up your dress, they’d have clothespins and safety pins up and down your back. They’d have strings that wouldn’t show to hold the movement of the skirt. The whole thing was absolutely ghastly. With Dick it was always movement. And I was young enough to walk out on one of the gargoyle heads of Nôtre Dame. Nobody else would do that. I was young enough to go out on high heels on one of those beams of the Eiffel Tower. I did roller-skating on cobblestones. He would set up these crazy situations.” Penelope Tree, one of his favorites in the sixties, says that “when you worked with Dick, you were so caught up in the moment, some intensely personal sort of moment. I’ve never had that experience with any other photographer before or since. It was really like having a love affair, except it wasn’t at all physical.”

The back wall, behind the Versace paraphernalia, is crowded with images of a different sort. Above low bookshelves filled with art books are framed photographs by Baron de Meyer, Atget, Brassaï, Man Ray, Cameron, and Avedon, most of them of disturbed-looking women. Also an Avedon portrait of his father that was the poster for his 1974 show at the Museum of Modern Art, and one of his horrific images of a grimacing Oscar Levant, which Avedon sometimes considers his finest portrait. The dark side of the Avedon psyche is in command here. (Avedon: “It is through the dark part of the eye that we see light.”) Nearby on the side wall is a huge blowup of four grimy coal miners, from the American West series. “I like that one less and less,” he says. “My hand is just too strong in it. Just too much of me manipulating. The craftsmanship, the composition. It’s all too apparent. It doesn’t reach below the surface.”

He laughs and makes a sweeping gesture that somehow includes the room and everything in it. “You know what I’m going to do? Empty this place out. Put everything on the walls in boxes, or the warehouse or the fire. I’ll just dump everything and start again, see who I become. Try to do it better, more deeply, and if I lose it, hope that my friends shoot me or at least stop me from becoming Steichen, photographing the apple tree outside my window with a new young wife kneeling at my feet.”

There’s a brick fireplace that Avedon never uses because pigeons have nested in the chimney. The mantel is cluttered with stuff, like every other flat surface here. An empty bottle of 1923 Lafite-Rothschild, Avedon’s birth year, stands on a boxed bottle of the same vintage, undrunk, “waiting for the right occasion.” There are also three parcels in brown wrapping paper, tied in ordinary string, unopened. He knows what one of them is—a bleached-white skeleton of a bird’s wing that washed up on the beach of Antigua years ago, during a photographic shoot with Suzy Parker; Dick and Suzy both wanted it, and it became their “bone of contention,” which travels back and forth between them. The other two boxes, he says, “I hope to open just before I die. They’re from someone who means a great deal to me. If I’m alone when I die, opening them—discovering what’s in there—will be like the right person holding my hand.”

It’s a quarter to twelve, way after his bedtime. He wakes up at five every morning, gets out of bed at six, turns the coffee on, and does last night’s dishes “for therapy.” Breakfast is coffee and fresh apple juice, squeezed by Verlie from whole apples the day before. His personal trainer comes three mornings a week at 7:30 to give him a one-hour workout. When he says good night, his voice is a little raspier, but his restless energy shows no signs of flagging.

It’s the next morning, 7:30, and Avedon is calling in great agitation. He says last night’s interview “didn’t work,” and we have to try again. This time he’ll invite his old and close friend Twyla Tharp, and he tells me I can be a fly on the wall while they wing it conversationally. OK, I say, well aware that there’s no arguing with Avedon in his control-freak mood. I go, I listen, I’m charmed, I’m well fed—lamb roast and applesauce with horseradish, homemade pumpkin pie and the usual cornucopia of desserts. His son, John, is there, and John’s nearly three-year-old son, Michael. So are the seventeen candles, which almost send the bamboo tree up in flames. It’s a warm, family sort of evening, and the conversation goes off in two dozen directions, and if it were reproduced here, we could have yet another portrait of Richard Avedon. The possibilities are endless. •

#6644. The Best Oxford Shirt for Men in 2026, According to GQ

The story behind the Oxford shirt is a lot less thrilling than you’d expect. It didn’t earn that fancy-sounding sobriquet through some sacred connection to the tony British university; instead, the shirt's signature cotton fabric was just one of four named after a group of schools picked by a Scottish mill for their associations with society’s upper crust. (19th century marketing at its best!)

But of the quartet—the others were Harvard, Cambridge, and Yale, FYI—only the Oxford shirt achieved menswear icon status, becoming a quintessential emblem of American prep as a “sporting shirt” and then as a staple of casual attire. Nowadays, Oxford-cloth shirts come in every color imaginable, but none of ‘em look quite as classic as the OG—especially when they’re thoroughly worn-in and a little wrinkled. Below you’ll find 16 of our absolute favorites, each one more ready than the last to imbue your jeans, chinos, and trousers with the unmistakable swagger of adopted American royalty.

J.Crew’s Oxford shirts have been a staple of the catalog for decades and though its iconic Secret Wash shirts are the bestsellers of the bunch, we prefer its more recent release, the 1983 Oxford Shirt. It’s easy to miss the differences at a glance, yet the handful of subtle tweaks add up quick. First, the fit: a comfier, more relaxed silhouette that, despite its ‘80s reference, is spot on for 2027. Second, the fabric: a noticeably sturdier, heftier all-cotton Oxford that makes its best-selling Secret Wash shirts feel wimpy by comparison. Third, and most importantly, the collar: unlike its most popular shirts, the 1983 Oxford has a satisfyingly taller collar with a prep-approved collar roll. It gives the shirt more life and more nuance, but also looks great under a blazer.

If there’s any brand that could do the Oxford justice, it’s the British label, Drake’s, known for its none-too-posh take on all things tailoring. Its handsome entry into the Oxford shirt ring is a confluence of top-shelf materials and methodical construction, wrapped into a single shirt worth saving up for. Handmade in Somerset, England, Drake’s Oxford features single-needle construction with finished seams throughout, which takes the cut and sew process twice as long to complete—on top of the high-density stitching you’ll find throughout the shirt. Lustrous mother-of-pearl buttons make for a luxe upgrade while the collar—a button-down with a fabulous collar roll—is constructed with a floating interlining to give it a soft structure.

All in, Drake’s Oxford is what most other Oxfords aspire to be. And if you’re curious about what comes after J.Crew, this is your answer.

Wythe’s built its brand on western aesthetics with lasting quality—think properly-made cowboy boots, Yellowstone-worthy coats, and snap shirts. That the label would produce something as east-coast as an Oxford shirt is head-scratching. And yet, it’s one of the best versions we’ve tried. That’s because Wythe takes the same sort of rigor that it uses for its western and workwear garments and applies it to the preppy classic. This as close as anyone can get to a deadstock Oxford shirt plucked from a long-forgotten storage room. From the box pleat and locker loop to the unstructured long-point button-down collar, size-stamped collar stand and nostalgic paper packaging, it’s a good reminder of why prep in the ‘60s was so, so good.

Plain Oxford shirts too simple for your liking? Thom Browne's take isn’t overtly avant-garde, but it does boast a striped grosgrain placket that shows itself when you undo the top or bottom buttons, a stitched-on tag near the right hip, and a similarly striped locker loop beneath the collar. Each one is made in Italy from a soft, durable cotton fabric with noticeable cuffs and a sharply curved hem, making this iteration a better fit with sleek dress pants or even your most refined athleisure. (Talking to you, sneakers-with-suit crowd.)

This shirt won’t win you any browny points with the tailoring nerds, it will earn you cred with the fashion elite.

For the guy who’s quick to chat your ear off for 20 minutes when all you said was, “nice pants”, Jake’s is the go-to shirt whisperer. Jake’s began as founder Jake Wigham was amidst his studies at the London College of Fashion, honing his skills at a tailoring apprenticeship and fulfilling custom projects. It eventually blossomed into the talk of the menswear cognoscenti, who praised Wigham’s shirtmaking prowess. Each shirt is made-to-order, cut and sewn in the Jake’s studio by a small team of expert craftspeople, according to your specific measurements, with options for different collars, pockets, and fabrics. While we’ll always respect the old guard shirtmakers who’ve honed their style over generations, Jake’s bridges the gap between traditional craft and modern appeal—a Savile Row approach that speaks internet.

According to menswear lore, Brooks Brothers is responsible for bringing the Oxford shirt stateside. Quite a few decades later, everything’s still here, from the telltale collar to the button cuffs, patch pockets, and curved hems. One note: Brooks Brothers says it’s a ‘regular fit’, but there’s a bit more room in the chest than some of its counterparts.

Japan's obsession with Americana often comes full circle, as is the case with Kamakura. Its shirts are the envy of so many labels for its craftsmanship which parallels that of custom shirtmakers. We're talking mother-of-pearl buttons, high-density stitching, and major attention to minor details like the roll of the collar and single-needle seams.

Gitman Vintage's stateside-produced shirts have been a fixture of tasteful menswear shops for years not only for its high quality control, but for its tailored silhouettes and idiosyncratic details like chalk buttons, its signature contrasting horizontal bottom button hole, and soft collars.

J.Press's take on the Oxford shirt stands out as among the preppiest examples. Not only does it come from the storied uniform supplier of Yale's student body, but the perfectly rolled collar and flap chest pocket details give it a distinctly collegiate look that would pass muster on any Ivy League campus.

The Clark shirt is one of Proper Cloth's best selling shirts thanks to its beefy Oxford cloth material, bewilderingly good construction (felled seams, split yoke, unfused placket, shanked buttons), and near-perfect fit. For $125, you cannot get a better Oxford shirt. But you have to be willing to wait because every shirt is made to order and will take a couple weeks to get to you. If you can remember to think ahead and have some patience, it’s well worth the wait.

Swedish brand Rubato crafts its R Oxford less traditionally, but it’s no less an Oxford because of it. It might eschew the conventional button-down collar, but thanks its super-tight blue stripes, button cuffs, and a fitted body designed to look good tucked or untucked, it skews decidedly old-world. The real clincher though, is the fabric, a 100% Sea Island cotton so soft we keep trying to pet our computer screen.

With a nerd-satisfying 22 stitches per inch, troca shell buttons, and other refined details, you’d be forgiven for thinking this shirt was made on Jermyn Street, famed for its shirtmaking history. But Sid’s shirts are proudly made in Honduras which makes them a great value compared to the British alternative.

Todd Snyder's lightweight Oxford shirt takes the OG and makes it even more casual, a perfect piece for layering over a graphic tee thanks to its relaxed fit and feather-light cotton fabric.

The quality of an Oxford shirt comes down to the fabric, construction, fit, and collar. They’re a distinct kind of button-up that warrants its own buying guide separate from dress shirts. Why? There’s so much history behind the style and the fabric.

Oxford cloth is beefier than a typical dress shirt fabric with more texture and thus has a more casual quality befitting of rumpled chinos and sneakers, territory most dress shirt fabrics would feel absolutely out of place. Seph Skerritt, CEO of Proper Cloth, says “You can think of it as a tougher, more durable and more casual cousin to the pinpoint dress shirt.” The cotton yarns are thicker than broadcloth, twill, and poplin, so the hand is noticeably less fine. The heftier material means a high-quality Oxford cloth is more durable and can even last as long as a decade.

Construction-wise, you should typically look for the same sort of details as you would with other dress shirts. Clean stitches, felled seams, buttons properly sewn with shanks, and reinforced at the side seams. High-quality Oxford shirts will also feature a split yoke which is the panel that spans the shoulders and is cut on the bias to give the area natural stretch for ease of motion.

Fit is subjective, of course, but you want to make sure that the shoulder seams line up with your natural shoulders, if not a little below for a relaxed fit. The chest shouldn’t pull, but shouldn’t feel like a potato sack. As for the body, this is more or less subjective and delves into the kind of silhouette you’re after, but if the fabric is pulling around the buttons, your shirt is too tight. And, depending on whether you like to tuck, should be long enough.

Oxford cloth shirts can come in any variety of collars, but the most common are button-down, spread, and point collars. Big menswear nerds will obsess over finding the perfect collar roll, a detail found in the golden age of Ivy style by the likes of Brooks Brothers and J.Press.

Oxford shirts are near and dear to our hearts. They’re classic, versatile, and durable—true staples that every guy should have. So we had opinions on what we wanted out of them. It all starts with the star of the show—the titular fabric. The Oxford cloth has to be meatier than the average dress shirt and with some noticeable texture. They should ideally be able to rumple more than crease and wrinkle.

From there, we looked for Oxfords that are well-constructed with beautiful buttons and, crucially, handsome collars. And because you can be surprised no matter how much you’re paying, we looked at Oxfords in all price points to find the best ones regardless of the tag.

So we looked to the seasoned veterans that built the Oxford’s reputation as well as the newcomers that are pushing it into the 21st-century as well as the runway designers that have let their imaginations run wild.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6642. The Best Veterans Day Food Freebies, From Dunkin’ Donuts To Shake Shack Burgers

A guide to the restaurants thanking veterans with free meals and treats.

Every November 11, Americans celebrate and thank those who have served in our military. Veterans Day marks the anniversary of the 1918 armistice that ended World War I, but it wasn’t until 1954, after both World War II and the Korean War, that it changed nationally from Armistice Day to Veterans Day.

To mark the occasion, many of our favorite national food chains are dishing out free meals, drinks, and treats to both active-duty military and vets. Here’s where you can score big.

Aroma Joe’s is offering veterans free handcrafted coffee or signature AJ’s Rush Energy Drink in any size up to 24 ounces at all locations with a valid ID.

Veterans and active-duty military members can get 10 free Boneless Wings + Fries with valid proof of service at participating BWW sports bars for dine-in only and GO locations with a minimum $5 purchase.

All active military members and veterans can enjoy a free All-American Single Smash or Americana Big Dog in-restaurant.

All active-duty service members and veterans with proof of service can enjoy a free Red, White, and Blueberry Pancake Combo that includes two buttermilk pancakes topped with glazed strawberries, blueberry topping, and whipped topping, along with two eggs, hash browns, and a choice of two strips of hickory-smoked bacon or two pork sausage links.

Active and retired military members can receive a free Original French Toast during operating hours for dine-in orders.

Active-duty, retired military members, and veterans can enjoy a complimentary order of Bang Bang Shrimp and a nonalcoholic beverage when dining at any Bonefish Grill location.

All active and retired military can enjoy a free donut.

All active military and veterans can receive a free single ShackBurger with a valid military ID or proof of service.

All active-duty and retired military members can enjoy a free meal from the chain’s special Veterans Day menu, with the purchase of a beverage when dining in at participating locations. The menu includes the option of 10-Piece Original Wings, Cheeseburger, Buffalo Chicken Sandwich, or Chicken Caesar Salad.

The bagel chain is offering veterans and active military a free coffee and bagel with schmear all day long. The offer includes any size hot or iced coffee and any bagel with any schmear and is only available in the bakery.

Gold Star Families, active military, veterans, and first responders can get a complimentary 5-Course Teppanyaki Entree, including a choice of Hibachi Steak, Chicken, or Salmon. The offer is available for dine-in only and requires the purchase of an appetizer or starter.

Veterans and military members can order a free Spaghetti with Marinara or Meat Sauce with proof of veteran or military status by using the code VET26.

All current and retired military members can enjoy a complimentary buffet and beverage at Golden Corral locations nationwide.

Active-duty military and veterans can enjoy a complimentary choice of 10 Bone-In or Boneless Wings, Beer-Battered Fish & Chips, Steakburger, Chicken Caesar Salad, Buttermilk Crispy Chicken Sandwich, or Chicken BLT Tacos.

Veterans and active military personnel can enjoy a free small hot or iced coffee and a free donut of their choice.

Service members and veterans can receive a complimentary entrée and beverage from a special prix fixe menu, plus a Buy One Get One card, good for a pizza, pasta, or salad with the purchase of one on a return visit between November 12 and 25.

Veterans with a valid military ID can receive a complimentary meal at participating locations when dining in the restaurant between 11 a.m. and 7 p.m.
