#6614. Best Men’s Winter Parkas 2026: 17 Heavy-Duty Snow-Busting Coats

The best men's parka is a lot like an upright sleeping bag, except it doesn't simply keep you insulated. It also protects your frostbite-prone fits from Mother Nature’s icy clutches, and keeps you looking sharp in the process. Don't believe us? Just ask the parka's most loyal servant: Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher.

Before giving you our favourites, some quick history: Parkas originated in the Arctic, where the Inuit designed them to withstand bone-chilling temperatures. They then made their way to the US military with the introduction of the N-3B parka in the 1950s. Throughout its evolution, the parka's mission has remained unchanged: to keep not just your torso warm, but your thighs and rear end too. Seriously, you've already worn that waist-length puffer to death: Make like Justin Jefferson. Go long.

The North Face McMurdo down parka isn’t just another winter coat—it’s a cold-weather icon with Antarctic-level credibility. Named after McMurdo Station, the US research hub in Antarctica, this parka is designed to thrive in below-freezing temperatures while keeping you comfortable and protected. With 600-fill recycled down insulation and windproof, waterproof, and breathable DryVent technology, it’s eco-friendly armor for the tundra—or the Target parking lot. Made from recycled nylon and polyester, it’s part of The North Face’s recycled-repurpose collection, combining sustainability with serious performance.

Loaded with features like six exterior pockets, a removable faux-fur ruff, an adjustable hood, and a draft flap, this 3.5-pound powerhouse is your portable fortress of warmth. Stylish touches like the midnight petrol color elevate it above standard winter fare, while practical details make it indispensable for everything from scraping windshields to tackling arctic adventures. Whether you’re braving brutal weather or commuting in comfort, the McMurdo is built to last—complete with The North Face’s warranty to keep it in the game longer than your ever-disappearing gloves.

Mountain Hardwear has been a staple in the outdoor gear world long before its sold-out collaboration with Stüssy (though they’ve probably gained a few new fans in the process). Founded in 1993 in Richmond, California, the brand spun off from the well-known outdoor company Sierra Designs. A group of designers and engineers left Sierra Designs to create Mountain Hardwear, and 32 years later, it’s still famous for its technical outerwear, sleeping bags, and pioneering use of Gore-Tex.

This jacket is built for camping, featuring a durable ripstop shell and 650-fill down. With a fully adjustable insulated hood and a drawcord at the waist to trap in heat, it’s tough to top even before you encounter the two BYO-bevvy pockets—specially designed to carry your favorite beverages. Whether you're in your tent or Air Streamer, this jacket keeps you warm—and your drinks cold—so you can stay cozy and hydrated in style.

Woolrich: So good it doesn't need a logo patch. The American outdoor company was founded in 1830, and since then has become the destination for warmth-minded men who don't need anyone else to know they're walking around in the very best materials.

Which isn't to say this parka won't turn some heads. New for this season, it comes in seven colors, from a stunning light blue to nutty falcon brown, and also boasts some envy-inducing hand-warmer pockets, hidden rib-knit cuffs, and even a water-repellent finish. (A nice touch for a style that typically is more preoccupied with keeping out the cold than the wet.) One more thing: It's called the Cloud because it's incredibly light, even with a 90/10 duck down fill. A winter coat that wears like a summer-weight hoodie? Worth the investment.

This is the kind of Canada Goose jacket that reminds you why the brand is so much more than just a status symbol for finance guys. (Though I'm sure they don't mind being that too.) For one, it's done away with that ubiquitous blue and red logo, and replaced it with a more understated, tonal patch. But that's actually the only thing that's been stripped back here: Otherwise, this parka is packed full of features, from ribbed knit cuffs, to pockets everywhere you look, to a bevy of insulation considerations, from the 625 Fill Down interior all the way to the soft, lined chin guard—a nice touch.

Available this season in Black, Olive, and Desert Sand (above), it's backed by Canada Goose's lifetime guarantee. So, yes, you're spending a fortune. But the brand stands ready to make sure you'll never need to buy another parka again.

The Japanese label FrizmWORKS has reimagined a classic, ‘60s‐era expedition parka silhouette—quilted down, hard-wearing cotton-blend shell, boxy hooded cut—and, sixty years later, given it a whole new life. From the tonal matte finish to the utilitarian drawcord hem, this is a mountain‐camp relic reimagined for your 2025 commute. It’s rugged without resorting to SSX Tricky branding, and along with the requisite down filling also has two fun, unexpected and large pockets on the back. It also comes in a joyful orange color, if that black is a little too subtle for you.

I can't be the only one who was excited to see Reigning Champ get back into making real clothes. (Though, let’s be honest, the brand’s sweatsuits are still some of my favorites.) But this high-powered, goose-filled nylon parka? It's built for Canadian winters, which means it’ll easily thrive anywhere else, too. Technically, that means 700 fill power down, and a weather-repellent nylon shell to keep out wind and rain, as well as the colder temps. Its defining feature is its stealthy, all-black appearance, and Reigning Champ has leant hard into that vibe, with hidden interior pockets, concealed rib cuffs, and a shock cord hood that you can pull as tight as you like. Now you see me, now you don't.

The new kids on the parka block, Big Rock Candy Mountaineering, are bringing the fun back with their vibrant, winter parka colors. These extreme cold-weather parkas take inspiration from mid-century American outdoor brands. Can’t think of any off the top of your head? Skim through a book like this, and you’ll catch the vibe.

BRCM’s parkas are packed with cozy duck down and feature a 100% grosgrain shell. This ribbed texture, courtesy of its tight weave, makes the fabric tough as nails and resistant to wear and tear. The ginormous pockets? Perfect for stashing your winter accessories (or your snacks). And if the wind has you feeling like it’s got something to prove, just tighten up the drawstring waist, hood, and hem. One of the coolest features? The jacket’s silhouette. When cinched, you can clasp your bag around the waist—ideal for those who love a good backpacking adventure. Although BRCM is still a fresh face in the outerwear world, it already feels like an instant classic.

Getting your hands on one of the first-ever parkas is basically impossible—right up there with finding your keys when you’re already late. Enter The Real McCoy’s, which somehow pulls it off with museum-grade reproductions. Every detail is obsessively dialed, down to the DuPont-developed nylon shell that helped kick off the whole modern-materials era.

Today’s outdoor companies are still trying to capture Patagonia’s lightning-in-a-bottle formula from when the brand first burst onto the scene: Be nice to everyone, make products the right way, and design jackets built to last forever. Take its Glacier parka, for example: it’s weatherproof, cozy enough to double as a sleeping bag, and so comfortable you might consider skipping the tent altogether.

If you’re after a quieter, minimalist parka—and you’ve got the budget—the Therme Parka delivers. It’s hip-length, packed with goose down, and built with the brand’s more environmentally friendly GORE-TEX ePE fabric, meaning it’s primed to handle a lifetime of winters.

The Alpha Industries N-3B is the real-deal snorkel parka—because it is the real deal. Produced early in the company's history in the 1950s, the parka is still tough as nails and loaded with reinforced elbow patches, a full-length storm flap, and snug inset knit cuffs that keep wind firmly in its place.

Founded in 1960, Fjällräven are sort of Sweden's Patagonia. By which we mean they've always thought about three things: High-performance materials, a reasonable enough price point, and dressing it all up in some great primary colors.

Nanga is your favorite outerwear brand’s favorite outerwear brand. Its parka riffs on the US Air Force’s N-3B flight jacket, upgraded with AuroraTex—a high-performance fabric that keeps you dry no matter what. Add handwarmer pockets and a discreet cigar pouch, and you’ve got a parka that nails the perfect blend between utility and style.

Goldwin is so good, it literally owns the North Face in Japan. (Like, literally.) This handsome down parka is wind-blocking, body-warming, and equipped with a PERTEX Quantum ripstop lining (and shell) to prevent the tears and rips that lightweight fabrics can otherwise be prone to.

Berghaus' Meru jacket—which is long enough to qualify as a parka in our book—is packed with retro styling, from the color blocks to the cinchable waistband. 2L Gore-Tex means you could wear it up any peak, but its general aura means you could also wear it up on stage, hands behind your back, tambourine on your head.

Montbell's mastery of lightweight, easy-to-rock, nicely-priced outdoors gear has become its calling card, and it’s on full display here. This down parka is easy to incorporate into pretty much any wardrobe, and even has some nice-looking stitching (which, by the way, the heads call ‘baffling’).

What do you get when you cross a parka with a fireman jacket? A full-scale compliment magnet.

First and foremost: functionality. A great parka should incorporate more features than a midnight infomercial. In the outer shell, you’ll typically find materials like nylon or polyester, and sometimes more rugged options like Gore-Tex. But it's also worth peeking under the hood—literally. Parkas are usually filled with down (duck or goose feathers) or synthetic insulation like polyester. Down is warm and lightweight, but it’s the fair-weather friend of insulation—it falters when wet. Synthetic insulations, on the other hand, is the ride-or-die option, keeping you warm even when soggy.

Hoods are another essential feature. Most will be made of a weatherproof fabric, and some come equipped with fluffy genuine- or faux-fur trims that gently tickle your face with a touch of winter luxury. And then there are the pockets—no one wants to walk around in a blizzard with frozen fingers. (Look for fleece linings.) Finally, asses the length. Longer parkas offer more warmth and protection from the elements, while shorter ones are perfect for commuters who need to dodge frostbite without overheating on the subway.

While function is the defining characteristic of a good parka, a great one should also give your winter fits a serious upgrade. Pair it with a thermal and a chunky sweater for a no-brainer look, or go bold by layering it over a denim jacket, adding corduroys, and anchoring with sturdy boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6611. King Charles Celebrates His 78th Birthday With Elton John

The two talked modern music, the King’s Trust, and more

The king is officially 78! Charles III, who was born in 1948—just four years before his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, took the throne—celebrated another trip around the sun today. And while the official birthday celebration of the monarch falls in June with the annual Trooping the Colour military parade, the royal family marked his real date of birth with a new portrait of him and Sir. Elton John.

The photo was taken during the taping of a special edition of John’s Apple Music 1 radio show, Rocket Hour, in which the “Tiny Dancer” musician was joined by Charles to mark 50 years of the King’s Trust charity. And in addition to discussing the nonprofit, the two also chatted about modern music, introduced over a dozen hand-selected tracks, and joked about aging.

“We and the Trust are definitely still standing,” the king teased, highlighting the Grammy-winning singer’s “I’m Still Standing” as one of his favorite songs. The musician, from his seat at the table, replied, “I’m still sitting now, though.”

At one point, the monarch gave a particular shoutout to Raye, who he said he “had the pleasure of being introduced to” during a “very memorable performance” at Apple.

A key focus of the Rocket Hour podcast has been to champion emerging artists—a mission that resonates with the King’s Trust’s focus on supporting the next generation. Formerly known as the Prince’s Trust, the organization was founded in 1976 to help young people facing unemployment, homelessness, academic troubles, and more. John has celebrated the charity’s milestones before, even performing at Wembley Arena for the 10th anniversary (1986). In 2001, he joined the royal family for a 25th anniversary dinner at St. James’s Palace in London.

“We are so richly blessed with the talents of our musicians, singers, and performers, particularly yourself, if I may say so,” the king continued, turning to his host. “You’ve become such a national treasure.”

He first showed off his fuzzy upper lip in mid-October at the 6th Annual Academy Museum Gala, where it was barely a whisper. By last night, it was fully formed, a couple weeks shy of hitting Tom Selleck-levels of bushy.

The actor gathered with a who’s who of young breakout talents named in GQ’s annual Man of the Year issue at the Sheats-Goldstein residence Wednesday night in Los Angeles to celebrate their spotlight-stealing achievements in entertainment, music, podcasting, and more. Cameli, for example, had a major moment as a lovable (and yes, hot) hockey player in Amazon’s hit television show Off Campus.

The fashion crowd has been embracing a hairy upper lip of late, and for good reason: When styled appropriately and kept tidy, mustaches go a long way to channel charm, confidence, and sex appeal. They also lend wearers a touch of maturity.

That might explain why there was no shortage of mustaches at last night’s bash. Fellow Breakouts member Stavros Halkias kept his signature handlebar look for the event, paired with some light stubble, while musician 54 Ultra matched his full-bodied mustache with an equally on-trend shag mullet and a healthy dosage of chest hair peeking from his unbuttoned dress shirt.

The prominence of scruff, stubble, and ’staches was a clear sign that facial hair isn’t going anywhere soon. If anything, it’s the breakout grooming look of the year.

#6609. Inside the New La Perla

La Perla’s comeback story isn’t a nostalgia play. CEO Alessio Vannetti recognizes that while people love vintage La Perla robes and bras, and past iconic brand moments like Halle Berry’s orange bikini in Die Another Day and Margot Robbie’s silk camisole in The Wolf of Wall Street, he’s on a mission to make modern-day La Perla just as famous.

“I want to do the best new lingerie ever. I want new generations looking at La Perla, not just for the vintage. I want the new generations purchasing totally brand new styles,” Vannetti says, speaking over Zoom from the brand’s Bologna, Italy, headquarters. “I think creativity should always lead.”

Vannetti, who became CEO of La Perla on September 1, is bullish on the lingerie brand’s prospects. Launched in 1954 by Ada Masotti, the brand became synonymous with luxury lingerie and was known for its handcrafted lacework, made by artisans in Bologna. By the 2010s, however, focus drifted as management changed hands. In 2023, La Perla was declared insolvent, and its factory went dormant. But its lace-trimmed lore lived on in pop culture: in the past few years, the brand got mentions in episodes of Emily in Paris and The Gentlemen, and Rosalía released a song called “La Perla” on her album Lux.

In 2025, La Perla was purchased by a white knight investor: entrepreneur and former Expedia CEO Peter Kern and his wife Kirsten swooped in to purchase the brand, its atelier and its former factory. They rehired all the artisans, and put a plan in place to bring La Perla back. That led to the hiring of Vannetti –– who has spent his career in brand and communications roles at houses like Gucci, Valentino, Zegna and Prada –– and a return to Milan Fashion Week with Collection #00 in September.

A new swimsuit collection will be shown later this month, to be available just in time for next summer. And La Perla’s e-commerce site is up and running, while Vannetti is scoping out revived wholesale partnerships with department stores and specialty boutiques, as well as potential store locations in the US, a top-priority market.

“Everything is new, and at the same time, everything is about reclaiming our original positioning,” says Vannetti. “How many times can you say that you are running a kind of startup, but with a brand equity as big as La Perla’s?

Where did La Perla go wrong? In part, Vannetti says, the company had pushed the brand to move faster than a high-luxury lingerie brand should. “My ambition is to create a profitable company, growing at the right speed, without compromising on quality or innovation,” says Vannetti. “In the first interview Ada Masotti gave when she founded the brand, she said that La Perla does not compromise on these two points. This is exactly what we are doing.”

Expansion at all costs is where compromise tends to happen. The brand is taking a slow approach: opening in new markets and with retail partners in order to contain that. Because lingerie is such a personal garment, he says, customers will immediately clock when the quality has gone down. “And they stop purchasing,” he says. “This is what happened in the past.”

La Perla’s production quality, after all, is its competitive edge. When the Kerns bought the company, they also bought the atelier and the factory, reviving the technique that Masotti created, on machines specific to La Perla. “She modified the machines in order to get a different stitch, and those modified machines are what have been preserved today,” Vannetti says. To keep that savoir-faire part of the brand’s secret sauce, La Perla will launch an academy in Bologna, where workers will train a new generation of sewers on techniques like frastaglio (where lace is inlaid on delicate silk or tulle) and macramé, as well as to maintain the machines should they need repair.

“We are not a public company, so we can really go at our speed, and our speed is not going to be extremely fast. It’s going to be La Perla speed,” Vannetti says. The brand has already designated the number of pieces it will produce for the next year, and it won’t exceed that. (He won’t say how many.) “I am 100% sure that by July, we will have the temptation. And that is the moment where I have to say, ‘OK, let’s stick to the plan.’ Because if you stick to the plan, and you build a brand on solid foundations, that’s where you’re healthy.”

Until then, the brand will test demand via its e-commerce store. Over the summer, the brand invited more than 200,000 former clients to shop the new collection on a private e-commerce platform ahead of the full dot-com relaunch in October. Bras started selling out, and Vannetti says a brand might be tempted to refill stock to capture sales that would otherwise go unfulfilled by switching production to a shorter-lead model — three weeks, say, rather than La Perla’s typical three months.

The brand is also testing the waters via one retail partnership with Harrods. The brand hosted a trunk show at Harrods for 19 clients — “the revenue generated was astonishing,” Vannetti says, though, again, he won’t disclose any figures as it’s too soon after a three-year shutdown. Now, he says, Harrods is pushing the brand to reopen its concession with the store. “We are running after that; we are trying to be as fast as we can, but that is the power of a desirable brand — the feeling that clients are missing it.”

Stores are also part of the strategic plan, though Vannetti says it will only open in specific markets, starting with New York and Los Angeles. The brand once had 135 stores at its peak. “We will never be in that situation again.”

While the history of the brand is paramount to this new phase, Vannetti is adamant the future of La Perla is not steeped in its past. “We all want to stay away from nostalgia,” he says. “When memories become nostalgia, there is the feeling that you cannot create new memories.”

What will the new cultural touchpoints for La Perla be? Vannetti says he is in conversations with Hollywood stylists and studios to get celebrities wearing La Perla or to have La Perla mentioned in more shows à la Emily in Paris. He’s also considering collaborations with other brands or designers if it feels right. Newness is part of the plan: in the next year, 60% of revenue will come from the brand’s icons, or recurring pieces, while 35% will be from new or one-off products.

The brand is also benefiting from the halo effect of the bra trend that dominated runways during the Spring/Summer 2027 season, perfectly in sync with its return. “Our mantra is inside by tradition, outside by choice, which is basically saying that we don’t want to and we will never become a ready-to-wear brand. But today, the bra is becoming the new top.”

But don’t expect La Perla to fully embrace ready-to-wear. That’s another wrong step past ownership took, Vannetti says. “They went in the direction of trying to aggressively become a ready-to-wear brand.” It worked best when it partnered with designers like Jean-Paul Gaultier or Dell’Acqua. “Those two moments were very good examples of how to preserve the brand identity. When they tried to expand to many different categories, it didn’t work. I really just want to do the best lingerie ever. It’s kind of the art of lingerie, the way we are approaching the future.”

#6607. Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly’s Full Relationship Timeline

Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly have yet to define their relationship publicly, but the two stars have been spending plenty of time together.

The actress and musician were first linked in September 2026, when they were photographed together in New York City. Days later, a source told People that Johnson and Kelly, whose real name is Colson Baker, “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The two stars had known each other before, but according to the source, they became closer after attending Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in July.

Since then, Johnson has watched Kelly walk the runway in Milan, and sources have shared more about how their connection developed.

Below, everything we know about Johnson and Kelly’s rumored relationship so far.

Johnson and Kelly both attended Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s July 3 wedding at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

The two stars already knew each other, but a source close to Kelly told People in September that they “hit it off” at the wedding.

On September 28, a source gave Entertainment Tonight similar intel, telling the outlet that Johnson and Kelly “really connected at Taylor and Travis’s wedding.”

On September 12, Johnson and Kelly were photographed together in New York City, getting out of the same SUV and entering Swift’s Tribeca apartment.

Four days later, a source close to Kelly told People that Kelly and Johnson “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The source explained that Johnson and Kelly “started off as friends and were texting often, but now they’re spending more time together.”

“It’s a very new start, but they’re smitten with each other right now,” the insider added. “They haven’t put a label on their relationship yet. They are just seeing where spending time together will take them.”

A second source characterized things as “super casual” at that point.

On September 22, Johnson and Kelly both traveled to Italy for Milan Fashion Week and attended the same event.

Three days later, Johnson addressed the broader attention her dating life receives during an appearance on Vogue’s The Run-Through podcast, though she never mentioned Kelly specifically.

“Even if I go to dinner with my manager or my lawyer, it’s like, ‘Seen with mystery man,’” she said. “I also don’t care.”

When asked whether she ever feels compelled to correct speculation about her personal life, Johnson explained why she prefers not to engage with it.

“I think it’s just futile. People are gonna believe what they wanna believe, and I don’t have the energy to fight for that,” she said. “I would much rather focus on other things in my life. Every day, there’s something on the internet that’s ridiculous and true or not true, and I don’t care.”

On September 28, a source shared more about Kelly and Johnson’s relationship with Entertainment Tonight: “Dakota was the one who made the first move. He’s very shy around her, but he likes her a lot. It’s still new, but they’re having fun and seeing where things go.”

The insider added, “Dakota has been a fan of his music and has always found him cute. He likes her a lot, too.”

On October 19, a source close to Kelly told People that he and Johnson were spending more time together. “They have been out on dates that people don’t know about because there aren’t any photos.”

The insider said that they’re in the “dating phase,” and “aren’t ready to go official yet.”

“They both really like each other and have been seeing each other more frequently,” the source shared. “They haven’t put a label on their relationship yet, but they’re growing closer every time they hang out.”

In the past few months, they’ve especially connected over their “same dry and dark sense of humor,” the source said. “[They] make each other laugh.”

Days later, Kelly and Johnson were photographed out in Los Angeles on October 23. They first left a music studio together, riding off in Kelly’s red Maserati. That evening, they were seen together again, leaving the Chateau Marmont.

A source close to Johnson gave People an update on their dynamic on October 28. “She’s happy and enjoys spending time with him,” the insider said. “There’s a lot of chemistry and she’s been going to the studio with him while he works. For now, it makes her happy.”

On November 3, Kelly and Johnson were photographed leaving a restaurant in Calabasas, California, after a dinner date. They were smiling and talking to each other in the shots.

Two days later, on November 5, Johnson and Kelly stepped out for another evening together in Los Angeles, attending a Khaite dinner at Dan Tana’s in West Hollywood. For the occasion, Johnson wore a black Death Row Pictures zip-up hoodie over a lace-trimmed Valentino miniskirt, paired with knee-high Gucci boots and statement diamond jewelry. Kelly opted for a more casual look, wearing a green satin bomber jacket over a yellow hoodie and gray sweatpants.

The next week, Johnson and Kelly stepped out for another evening together in Los Angeles on November 11. The pair first attended a screening of Johnson’s short film Flesh Impact, before heading to dinner at the Tower Bar inside the Sunset Tower Hotel with friends. Kelly opted for a casual look while Johnson showed up in a satin corset-anchored sheer slip dress and floral mules.

They later made their way to Kelly’s recording studio, where they were photographed leaving shortly before 3 A.M. For the late-night outing, Johnson wore a more relaxed look with a standout tiger-striped Nour Hammour coat.

The following day, the pair was spotted outside of the studio again. This time, Johnson wore a floor-length black two-piece set with a floral pattern.

#6603. 43 Party Appetizers That Pack A Lot Of Flavor Into One Bite

Appetizers are even more delectable when you can gobble them up in one bite. You get all those mouthwatering flavors in one fell swoop, and we have you covered with some of our best bites (literally!). Whether you want fancy little puff pastry bites or the classics like stuffed mushrooms and bang bang shrimp, these bite-sized finger food recipes are going to be perfect for your next dinner party, game day tailgate, or holiday potluck.

Want to really impress your guests? Try our easy (yet impressive) apps that are sure to stun. Our recipes for cranberry brie wontons, Caesar salad deviled eggs, and candied bacon smokies are all easy to create, but wow a crowd every time.

With all these appetizers working their way around the room, you're going to need some cocktails and mocktails to go with them. Serving a crowd? Try one of our many big-batch cocktails so you can focus on your guests (and those apps!). Whatever you do, don't forget dessert either! These potluck-friendly dessert ideas will keep your spread looking like you hired a pro to do it.

These pumpkin Parmesan pinwheels strike the perfect balance of sweet, savory, and decadent. Store-bought puff pastry is the foundation of this appetizer. From there, we make a filling with canned pumpkin puree, Parmesan, and garlic to replicate the ravioli filling. There’s also some fresh chopped sage in there to double down on the fall vibes.

Baked feta pasta took the world by storm, and once we tried it, we knew we couldn’t stop at just the classic viral recipe. We created these baked feta bites to be the perfect no-fuss holiday appetizer, capturing all of the same flavors as the OG. Thanks to easy, store-bought ingredients, these flaky, flavor-packed bites are perfect for any last-minute party planning.

If your friends love our cranberry brie bites, they’ll go nuts for these cranberry brie wontons. Brushed with butter and air-fried until crispy on the outside and gooey in the middle, these wontons are the party snack you need this holiday season. Don’t forget the bowl of cranberry sauce for dunking—it makes it feel extra-festive.

Unsurprisingly, Caesar salad deviled eggs are just as delicious as their namesake. This is exactly the kind of app you need to make for your next girls’ night in or holiday party. Just be prepared for everyone to ask for the recipe.

Buffalo wings, take note—mozz tots are coming to steal your game day thunder. Breaded and fried 'til crispy and golden, these bite-sized cheesy nuggets are the must-make app your Super Bowl party needs.

While we love our Caprese skewers, we decided to use one of our favorite store-bought ingredients (puff pastry, of course) to transform these classic flavors into a new, poppable app: baked Caprese bites.

These shrooms are the definition of tiny but mighty: cheesy, garlicky flavor is packed into every bite of this poppable, bite-sized app. No matter the holiday or time of year, this is the easy and versatile appetizer we always turn to.

These are the perfect lazy-girl appetizer that won’t challenge your wonton-folding skills. Crab rangoon cups have all of the flavors and textures that make crab rangoon so irresistible without any of the feelings of failure that can come with a poorly assembled wonton pocket.

With the addition of pesto, grated Parmesan, and crushed red pepper flakes, these two-bite beauties transform from their standard pale yellow, paprika-dusted form to towering, bright green mini Christmas trees. Serve these at your next holiday potluck, brunch, or festive weeknight dinner when you can’t be bothered with real food.

Need a party app fast? This 5-ingredient recipe is IT. We wrapped bacon around Little Smokies, then sprinkled them with brown sugar for an upgrade to the classic game day appetizer that’s a must-make bite.

Our stuffed mushrooms are one of our most popular holiday appetizers, so it’s only natural that we create a fresh variation to take the texture to a new level. These bite-sized beauties are stuffed into a crispy sushi rice cup to add a little bit of crunch to an already perfect appetizer.

Looking for the easiest, most festive appetizer possible? We got you! You only need 4 ingredients and less than an hour to make some adorable holiday wreaths that could easily be at the center of your table.

If you’re looking for an easy, impressive app for this holiday season, you’ve got to make these brie bites. The flavor combination just makes sense—flaky puff pastry paired with nutty, buttery brie and drizzled with honey—and the method is so fun.

Bang bang shrimp will forever be one of my favorite appetizers. Crispy shrimp are the perfect vehicles for the sweet, sour, and spicy sauce that smothers their crispy outer coating, making it soft and crunchy all at once. This air fryer version makes these poppable bites almost too easy to enjoy.

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays, or really at any dinner party. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie.

Let’s talk about Domino’s stuffed cheesy bread—it's cheesy, herby, and downright irresistible. This recipe is a close approximation you can whip up at home, and dare I say, it tastes even better. Fair warning: This recipe calls for a lot of cheese.

If you have an unrelenting weakness for salty, cheesy, deep-fried snacks, then you’re in the right place. These pimento cheese-stuffed fried olives are the perfect finger food to satisfy any savory craving.

Buffalo sauce might be synonymous with wings and dip, but if you love it as much as we do, there’s no reason to relegate it to just game days and tailgates. These stuffed mushrooms are packed with Buffalo flavor, but wouldn’t look out of place at a dinner party or holiday celebration.

Just like our famous cranberry brie bites, these little guys are hard to put down! They're the perfect amount of sweet and savory, so you can serve them before or after a holiday meal.

We're sure you’ve heard of pigs in a blanket, but have you heard of pigs in a quilt? Here, we swap crescent dough wrapped around the hot dog with a quilt made with woven crescent dough. All you need is some hot dogs, classic crescent roll dough, and egg wash for a shiny golden finish.

#6602. The Stars Brought the Glamour to the 2026 Baby2Baby Gala Presented by Paul Mitchell

Harper’s Bazaar has exclusive snapshots from the event’s portrait studio

Every year, the Baby2Baby Gala brings together the biggest names in philanthropy, entertainment, and fashion for an evening of fundraising and celebration. And last night, the 15th edition was no exception—with the likes of Demi Moore, Andrew Garfield, Jessica Alba, Barbara Palvin and Dylan Sprouse, Kerry Washington, and Katy Perry showing up in West Hollywood to support the organization’s mission to help kids in need.

From the gala’s inception, Baby2Baby co-CEOS Norah Weinstein and Kelly Sawyer Patricof wanted to create an event that felt “less like a traditional fundraiser.” Year after year, the night has offered its star-studded guests more than just an excuse to get dressed up and a chance to make a difference with their wallets—pairing fundraising efforts with exclusive dining experiences from top chefs and intimate performances from award-winning musicians. (Last night, Carbone flew in from New York City and Cardi B took the stage.)

“We wanted to create an event that would appeal to a younger generation of donors through our approach to food, fashion, and celebrity, while making sure that nobody left the gala without understanding our mission,” Weinstein and Patricof told Harper’s Bazaar. “Fifteen years later, the gala has evolved in ways we never could have imagined, but some themes have stayed exactly the same. Every flower and fork is underwritten by our generous sponsors so that every dollar raised can go directly to Baby2Baby and the children we serve.”

Each year, the funds raised from the gala help get millions of basic essentials—from diapers to formula to clothing—to children who need them. But the organization, with an all-female board of directors, spends all year working towards the Baby2Baby mission. “The gala brings this extraordinary community together for one night, but it’s their commitment throughout the year that makes our work possible,” the CEOs shared.

Andrew Garfield is on GQ’s plush 2026 Men of the Year red carpet, his sandy mane slightly cropped, two beefy lapels spread across his chest. The Artificial protagonist, wearing Savile Row stalwart Edward Sexton, is one of the three co-hosts—alongside his fellow MOTY cover stars, Matt Damon and Chris Rock—of this year’s party at the Chateau Marmont, and his ultra-sharp lapels made him look every bit like the Hollywood powerhouse he is.

Garfield’s Artificial co-star, Yura Borisov, was also sporting a fat, wooly set of wings, courtesy of Dior. And then there was Belmont Cameli, one of our 2026 Breakouts, who shot to fame as the romantic lead in yet another steamy hockey drama to take over our screens this year, Off Campus. Proof that sometimes the difference between a good suit and a great one is larger-than-life lapels.

#6598. Who Is Elizabeth Holmes’s Partner, Billy Evans?

This story contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.

When Nathan Fielder asked Elizabeth Holmes to document the days leading up to her serving her prison sentence for his new A24 documentary, You Can See Everything, the proposition meant that he would also be spending a large portion of the shoot with Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans.

The documentary spends time delving into Holmes’s public legal scandal with Theranos—the now-defunct biotech company that saw her committing investment fraud—but it also sheds light on Holmes and Evans’s relationship and how they have managed to thrive despite her sentencing.

As the documentary, co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, progresses, Fielder’s focus shifts from Holmes to Evans. “Weren’t you worried she was scamming you?” Fielder asked him at one point, to which Evans responded, “100 percent, but what does she have to gain from me?” When presented with the knowledge of his family’s wealth, Evans defended Holmes and said, “I think there’s a lot of different levels of wealth.” Things only snowball from there.

Evans’s grandparents, William and Anne Evans, own the Evans Hotel Group. Founded in 1953, Evans Hotels consists of three luxury properties, which include The Lodge Terry Pines, the Bahia Resort Hotel, and the Catamaran Resort Hotel and Spa. All three of the properties are located in California.

Evans’s LinkedIn profile revealed that he attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology between 2011 and 2015. He earned his bachelor’s degree in economics.

Evans’s LinkedIn also revealed that he’s the CEO of Haemanthus, his self-founded AI-driven medical testing startup; he’s held the role since 2022. The company aims to achieve a mission similar to that of Holmes’s Theranos, which sought to provide blood diagnostics through one drop of blood with the Edison machine. Instead of using one drop of blood for diagnostics, Haemanthus is working to create a device that tests blood in addition to urine and saliva for the presence of diseases.

“This is not Theranos 2.0. Theranos attempted to miniaturize existing tests. Our approach is fundamentally different. We use light to read the complete molecular story in biological fluids, seeing patterns current tests can’t detect. Not an improvement. A different paradigm,” the company shared in a statement to Fortune in 2025, following reports of Holmes advising on the project. “Setting the record straight. Elizabeth Holmes has zero involvement in Haemanthus. We’ve learned from her company’s mistakes, but she has no role, now or future.”

In a 2023 joint interview with The New York Times, Evans revealed that he and Holmes fell for each other fast. “To say we immediately fell in love isn’t an overstatement,” he said.

Holmes, however, noted that Evans had some reservations about entering a relationship with her. “It had been two years of all this stuff written about me, and I think you get to know someone in a totally different way when you walk in with that skepticism versus if you meet when everything is sunshine and roses,” she said. “That allowed us to get to know each other in a really deep way.” The couple got engaged in August 2018.

Holmes gave birth to their son, William Holmes Evans, in 2021. By 2023, a court document revealed that Holmes gave birth to her and Evans’s second child, a daughter named Invicta.

Evans attended several of Holmes’s court dates, appearing by her side on the way to and from her hearings. In January 2022, she was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. She’s currently serving her sentence—which was reduced to nine years from 11 years—at Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Texas. She will be transferred to a halfway house in August 2027.

While Holmes was sentenced, Evans asked the court in November 2022 to shorten her sentence so she could enjoy more special moments with their son. “My heart is broken with the thought of spending any days away from Liz, for a future in which my son grows up with a relationship with his mother on the other side of glass armed by guards,” he said. Evans still visits Holmes regularly, with him telling People in February 2025 that it has been “hell and torture” at the prison facility. The tech CEO added that it “shatters” Holmes when she says goodbye to him and her family.

You Can See Everything makes some shocking revelations about Evans, like that he posts from Holmes’s X account while she’s in prison (for a while, it was without her knowledge), and that he arranged to be paid for his and Holmes’s appearance in the documentary, which he ultimately rescinded. (It’s unclear whether Holmes knew about the deal.)

During a screening of the film in L.A. this month, Fielder said of the couple, “Neither of them have seen the film. Elizabeth is still incarcerated; Billy hasn’t seen it.” He added, according to The Hollywood Reporter, that Evans “started trying to exert a level of control over the process that made it very hard to engage with him, and it was uncomfortable for us and also A24 and everyone. And I think we sort of had to stop—I think communication broke down basically, and we’ve been in that like state for a little bit. So it’s been challenging in that way.”

Evans confirmed that he hasn’t seen the film during an interview with the All In podcast, which was released on October 15. “I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said, per Variety. He has seen the trailer and said that Holmes “looks insane” in it. Evans added, “Am I nervous? I have been through so many intense, surreal experiences that it takes a bit to raise my blood pressure. With this, there’s certainly concern, but it’s ultimately our decision.”

On November 3, Evans revealed the “one misconception” about his relationship with Holmes following the release of the movie: “That I somehow control Liz. Anyone who actually knows her would find that idea hilarious,” he responded to an X user.

Evans added, “She’s fiercely independent, strong-willed, and my best friend. We are partners in every sense. We challenge each other, disagree, and face the world together. Her closest friends are also some of my closest friends. If I ever mistreated her, they’d have my head.”

In a separate tweet, Evans revealed that he misses “everything about [Holmes].” He wrote, “I miss her presence. Her touch. The way she runs her fingers through my hair. Her patience. She makes me a better person. And without her, I feel an emptiness that’s hard to describe. People often say they need someone when what they really mean is that they want them. I’ve thought a lot about that distinction. I need Liz. She should qualify as a medically necessary prescription.”

On All In, Evans elaborated on why he wanted to make the film ahead of Holmes’s 11-year sentence. “She’s been prevented from speaking publicly in any way, shape, or form, and this would come out after that period in which she is now allowed to talk,” he said. “There’s been a lot of media produced on her. There’s been a lot of people who have told her story. That narrative is pretty ossified. The whole idea was: Here she is, see her and make up your own mind. It’s not to re-litigate the case. Practically, at this time she was not allowed to talk about the case, so she was gonna follow the rules and not talk about the case.”

He explained that his own loved ones have thought he was “crazy” for knowing—and now being in a relationship with—Holmes. “And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift,” Evans said. “That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.”

On November 15, Evans spoke with CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman for his first television interview about You Can See Everything, which aired on CBS Sunday Morning. During their conversation, he addressed the documentary’s portrayal of him as controlling and manipulative, pushing back against the characterization. “I’m deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do, but no, I am not some controlling monster who’s leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I’m not those things,” he said.

Still, Evans said he did not regret participating in the documentary, even as he acknowledged the discomfort of seeing himself portrayed as a villain. “I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it’s entertainment,” he told Gutman. “I didn’t get to control the edit.” He added that his primary concern was how audiences would perceive Holmes. “I think that my goal is to have people see Elizabeth. And when I watch that movie, I see the person that I love in exactly who she is.”

When it comes to his personal agreement to participate in the project, he said, “I think sometimes I take too big of risks.” Then, when Gutman asked for an example, Evans replied: “Inviting Nathan Fielder into your home for 34 days and trusting somebody to have the right to portray you in any way, shape, or form that they so choose.”

He said choosing to do this interview with CBS was an attempt to get his voice back. “You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life….With Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is, ‘You can’t lose your voice.’”

During the interview, Evans also addressed the documentary’s controversial shower scene, in which he appears fully nude. He said he knew cameras were filming him but did not consent to the footage being shown. A24, the film’s production company, maintained that everything filmed was done with the couple’s consent.

Gutman also asked Evans about speculation that Fielder had developed romantic feelings for Holmes during filming. Evans disagreed with that interpretation, saying, “I think Nathan cares a lot about Elizabeth. And I didn’t get the impression for a minute that it was romantic.” When Gutman pointed to the scene of Fielder and Holmes playing in the water, Evans noted that he was nearby: “I was five feet to the right of them, also in the water.”

Evans further discussed the threats he says his family has received following the documentary’s release, calling them a “daily” and “terrifying” occurrence.

#6597. Hunter Schafer’s Blade Runner 2099 Press Tour Is Full of Vintage Finds and Colorful Statements

With custom Prada, Y2K Undercover, and straight-off-the-runway Lii

2026 has had no shortage of press tours. From The Devil Wears Prada 2 to The Odyssey to Euphoria to The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, it’s been a year of global rollouts and method dressing. And we’re not quite done yet.

Earlier this week, Hunter Schafer kicked off the Blade Runner 2099 promo at the Los Angeles premiere in a custom Prada leather micro dress and voluminous fur coat—and since then, she’s been bringing her A game to the miniseries’ press. Working with stylist Dara, the Euphoria actor has showed up in straight-off-the-runway pulls and vintage finds alike, piecing together a dynamic collection of ensembles as she counts down the days to the November 25 release date.

While the sci-fi series takes place some 73 years in the future, Schafer turned back a couple decades for the first day of her press junket. Working with Dara once again, the actor was seen wearing a full look from the Undercover Fall/Winter 2007 collection.

The Y2K ensemble was composed of a handful of neutral layers, including a turtleneck base, a long-sleeve ribbed knit top with sheer accents, and little micro shorts in chocolate brown. She wore ear muffs and her hair in pigtails, and tucked her semi-sheer thigh-high stockings into black-and-brown wedges.

Later, the star switched gears, selecting a vibrant color-blocked minidress from Zane Li’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection for Lii. The high-contrast runway piece saw a bright-teal shift dress with a square neckline and spaghetti straps, layered with an open-back coral-orange piece with a similar silhouette. (See photos here.)

Out at the end of the month, Blade Runner 2099 takes place half a century after the events of 2017’s Blade Runner 2049. The science-fiction limited series stars Schafer as Cora, a human fugitive posing as a Blade Runner, alongside Michelle Yeoh as Olwen, an aging Blade Runner facing death.

#6596. Joe Budden Can't Stop Betting on Himself

This is an edition of the weekly newsletter Tap In, GQ senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe’s final word on the most heated online discourse about music, movies, and TV. Sign up here to get it free.

There’s Joe Budden, and then there’s everyone else. Despite the proliferation of rapper-led podcasts and talk shows in the last few years (itself a subset of the ever-ballooning celebrity podcast bubble), there’s no question who leads the pack—at least that’s how Budden sees it. It’s hard to argue with him: in February, Budden’s self-titled and pioneering podcast will turn 12,. Not too long ago, he posted a screenshot that “accidentally” revealed his yearly take-home was a number in the low eight figures.

Through it all, there've been dramatic cast changes, tense moments with rappers, hilarious must-see breakdowns of big moments in culture, and several dust-ups with Drake, a frequent subject of Budden and his co-host’s. Being part-New Jerseyian, I’m one of the vocal minority that believe it’s a travesty to reduce Budden’s rap career to “Pump It Up” (this is never far from my Recently Played to this day). Our paths actually crossed during his time at Complex, when I served as a sit-in for test episodes of Everyday Struggle while he searched for the co-host that would eventually become Akademiks—and even helped them launch the show with a series of digital short skits I wrote and produced that are probably lost to the internet by now.

As an occasional pod listener, I find it fascinating that Budden has defied all odds, and everyone who said he was bound to burn bridges, and now finds himself commanding attention, revenue and even reconciliations with his past employers. Despite how things went with State of the Culture, he’s back in business with Revolt. Joe Budden Network Presents, his new weekly series, premieres on November 13th, bringing his podcast to linear television through a unique micro-licensing partnership that allows Joe to retain full ownership of his IP.

To mark his next chapter, we talked about the current landscape of rap media and podcasting, the dangers of getting too comfortable, and how he plans to maintain his reign.

#6595. Key Takeaways From Luxury’s Q3 Earnings

China’s macro environment has been a major drag on luxury’s third-quarter earnings, causing most companies to fall short of market expectations.

Analysts expected growth to slow in Q3, but conditions in China turned out worse than anticipated. The sector’s average organic sales growth ended at 4% in Q3 2026, versus 7.8% in Q2 (calculated by Goldman Sachs on the basis of a simple average of luxury companies, excluding currency impact).

Kering stock plummeted 17%, following the announcement that growth at the company had dropped to 1% in Q3 (vs +2% in Q2), including a 6% decrease at its largest brand, Gucci. (Gucci retail sales declined by 9% on a comparable basis.) Kering and LVMH stock are each down 37% year to date, while the Hermès share price has fallen 36%.

“Everyone is staying on the sidelines,” Goldman Sachs luxury analyst Erwan Rambourg says, referring to investors’ cautious stance. While he believes that Q3 marks the trough in the luxury downturn, he thinks that investors prefer to wait for tangible signs of an improvement rather than catch a falling knife.

And after a stellar performance in the first half of the year, jewelry brands began decelerating in Q3. Sales at Richemont’s jewelry maisons, including Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, rose 14% versus 24% in Q2. Sales at LVMH’s watches and jewelry division and Kering’s jewelry arm, the latter of which includes Boucheron and Pomellato, were up 6% and 11%, respectively (vs 11% and 18% in Q2). Sales at other Hermès sectors, including jewelry and home, were down 1% (vs 4% in Q2).

“Richemont’s jewelry maisons growing 14% in the fiscal second quarter is a slowdown, but it’s still tremendously better than pretty much anyone else in the sector,” Rambourg flags. “That gives a first-half average of just below 20% top-line growth for jewelry, which is the core profit driver of the company. For the first time in a while, margins have increased.”

Here are the rest of the key takeaways from luxury’s Q3 earnings.

China’s slowdown deepened after three years of deceleration. Growth at LVMH decreased 5% in Asia, while Kering fell 8% and Hermès came in flat. “It should be noted that the macroeconomic environment [in China] remains unfavorable,” Hermès’s VP of finance Eric du Halgouët told analysts during the company’s earnings call on October 22.

While the broader picture in China remained largely unchanged, with continued weakness in the real estate market, two additional factors weighed on bottom lines: the decline in equity market performance, and China’s new taxation of foreign assets. The law on taxation, which was announced in late July and applies to offshore trusts, a widely used vehicle among high-net-worth Chinese individuals, had a significant impact on the sentiment of affluent consumers; the rules have retroactive effect from 2023, and the deadline to declare and pay was just 90 days.

“The two growth engines of the industry for the past 20 years are the middle-income consumer and the Chinese consumer,” says Morgan Stanley managing director Édouard Aubin. These two engines are now barely running.

Using LVMH as a proxy, the Chinese cohort was flattish in Q2 and down approximately 15% in Q3. Richemont also highlighted the challenges in the mainland China market, despite seeing a positive trend in Greater China. “ If anybody thinks we’re less affected by [market conditions in] China, on the contrary,” chairman Johann Rupert told reporters during a media call on Friday.

Some soft luxury brands are still doing well, including in China. Ralph Lauren’s Asia revenue saw 28% growth in Q3. Greater China led retail growth for Burberry (+5%), and the Greater China region was up 5.7% for Zegna Group. In the private space, Chanel and Longchamp are also understood to perform well in China.

One category doing surprisingly well in China is prestige beauty. L’Oréal Group posted 7.8% growth in North Asia in Q3. “North Asia was back to high-single-digit growth for the first time since the first half of 2022. This marks a step change in L’Oréal’s growth algorithm in our view,” HSBC analysts, including Olivier Nicolaï, wrote in a note. Puig revenues rose 12.9% in Asia-Pacific. Does it suggest that Chinese customers are trading down — buying lower-ticket items like fragrances and skincare?

And is there a brighter outlook ahead for luxury brands in China? “There aren’t many hopes for things to improve in the short term,” Rambourg says. “I think China being very tough is probably going to be the case for the next two or three quarters. Visibility is quite poor. And if you leave aside bases of comparison, there’s no key underlying reason for China to do better.”

“Q3 was a continuation of the K-shaped economy we’ve seen in recent quarters — where the top end grows, but the lower end lags as the middle-income consumer has been priced out. The brands at the top of the pyramid are doing well; the rest are not,” Aubin says.

Zegna brand (+12.7% in Q3), Brunello Cucinelli (+13.5% in Q3), Loro Piana (“enjoying very strong growth,” according to LVMH CFO Cécile Cabanis) and Chanel (up double digits in Q1, Q2 and Q3, according to industry sources) are in the former category.

At LVMH, Cabanis noted that Louis Vuitton sales came in just behind the group’s fashion division at -5%, while Dior was flat. Rambourg remains bullish on Dior. “One, Dior is more exposed to China than some other brands, so that’s painful. Two, they have a men’s business, which is not doing as well as women’s. Three, I think it takes a bit more time for [creative director] Jonathan Anderson’s products to gain weight within the brand, but it’s certainly coming,” he explains.

Louis Vuitton felt the repercussions of both its legal dispute with Chinese tea brand Molly Tea and an issue with a shipping partner — the latter weighed on quarterly growth by a little over one percentage point. Add to that a tough year-on-year comparison basis: Louis Vuitton opened a boat-shaped mega-store in Shanghai in June 2025, dubbed The Louis, which generated a surge in foot traffic. The brand is undergoing a change in strategy, according to Rambourg: “They’re in the process of moving under the influence of deputy CEO Damien Bertrand, from what Louis Vuitton was 15 months ago, which was colorful, cheerful, fashion-driven, to something more institutional, more focused on the origin of the brand, which is the art of travel.”

A Shanghai Fashion Week attendee wears a full Louis Vuitton look.

Kering’s recent creative changes were on the agenda of the group’s earnings call. Shortly before its Q3 earnings, Kering announced the departures of Anthony Vaccarello from Saint Laurent and Seán McGirr from McQueen. And on November 5 and 6, the group announced the departure of Pierpaolo Piccioli from Balenciaga, with Martine Rose to succeed him.

While still outperforming the sector, Hermès’s growth decelerated in Q3 (+4.3% in Q3 vs +6.7% in Q2). “While Hermès’s leather goods category re-accelerated to nearly 11%, some investors questioned whether the weakness in other categories, such as ready-to-wear and accessories, could foreshadow a similar slowdown in leather goods,” Barclays director Carole Madjo says. Risk of [handbag market] saturation in China and the increasingly structured secondhand market could potentially weigh on demand over time.”

After years of Miu Miu outperforming Prada, the trend reversed in Q2, with Prada (6.3%) surpassing Miu Miu (2.6%), and continued into Q3, as Prada grew 1% while Miu Miu contracted 3%, likely due to a higher exposure to China and the Middle East  relative to the average of the sector.

Rambourg also stressed the important polarization across brands: “In the soft luxury space, we consider Chanel is now the biggest brand — bigger than Louis Vuitton — and growing very quickly. And so that’s taking a bit of the air from the others, notably adjacent brands like Hermès. In hard luxury, Cartier is continuing to do very well and is also taking a bit of air away from their competitors. So in both soft and hard luxury, you have one dominant brand which counterintuitively is growing very quickly.”

The US might remain a luxury growth driver, but things began to decelerate this quarter, partly because of a tougher comparison basis. Hermès was up 8.8% in the Americas in Q3 (vs 13.7% in Q2), and Kering’s North American retail revenue rose 1% (vs 10% in Q2). “Investors are questioning whether this signals the beginning of a normalization in the US, and whether it will be confirmed in Q4 and beyond,” Barclays’ Madjo says.

Goldman Sachs’s Rambourg dismissed concerns: “I do believe that the little softness in Q3 is temporary. I foresee a re-acceleration in Q4 linked to the easier comparison basis and the reality that holiday campaigns, new products and more thoughtful pricing should motivate people to buy. Not to mention that you had a lot of wealth creation from equity markets. Luxury demand has been a bit lagging, but I think it’s bound to pick up.”

It is unclear whether the US midterm elections — which saw the Democrats take control of Congress for the remainder of Trump’s presidency — impacted the third quarter. Some customers possibly adopted a wait-and-see approach to spending ahead of the results, which could now be released and influence Q4. “Midterm elections typically have less impact than presidential elections,” Madjo notes. Asked what impact the outcome might have on Richemont’s business, CFO Burkhart Grund said: “We’re just a few days after the midterm elections and we haven’t really picked up anything meaningful.”

Europe was up 4% for LVMH, down 5% for Kering’s fashion and leather goods division (including a 9% drop for Gucci), and up 7.2% for Hermès. “It is Europeans who are spending in Europe,” said Hermès’s Eric du Halgouët. Hermès’s sales in France decreased in Q3 to 3.6% from 6.2% in Q2, as the heatwave impacted footfall in the Parisian stores.

As brands began gearing up for the crucial holiday season, protests erupted across France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Portugal. France and Italy are significant European markets. France accounted for 8% of LVMH’s total revenue in the first nine months of 2026 and 9.6% of Hermès’s nine-month revenues. “The comments on the impact of the protests in Europe were quite vague. It’s too hard to say and hard to quantify,” Madjo says.

LVMH’s earnings call took place before the so-called Act I, the day of major urban unrest on October 17. On October 22, Hermès’s du Halgouët said it was too early to assess impact on local stores’ business and tourism. (The Hermès store in Marseille was looted and store windows in Paris, Nantes and Lyon were broken.) “It’s not just a China problem. Now, you have a French-Italian problem on top of that,” Aubin notes, referring to the possible effects on Q4.

Despite the lack of visibility in China and Europe, Goldman Sachs’s Rambourg anticipates a progression in Q4 and next year. “Because we see the US re-accelerating, and importantly, we see self-help measures — product launches and better pricing — motivating consumers to come back,” he says.

#6594. One-Pan Creamy Spinach-Artichoke Gnocchi

Out of all the party dips, spinach and artichoke reigns supreme in our book. While we’re all for a chip-and-dip dinner, that’s not the most family-friendly weeknight meal, so we turned it into this decadent pasta dish. We combined everything we love about our favorite dip—spinach, artichokes, cream & cheese—with quick-cooking gnocchi, turning it into an easy meatless dinner that’s loaded with flavor. It’s easy enough for when you’re just craving comfort food (just one pan!), but fancy enough to serve to guests too.

Top tips & variations:We added briny capers here to help cut through all the richness, but if you’re not a fan, feel free to skip. While the gnocchi simmer, stir to prevent sticking, and try to keep them in an even layer so they stay submerged and cook evenly. The recipe calls for marinated artichokes because they’re already flavored with ingredients like garlic and red pepper, but canned or frozen will work in a pinch too.

It’s up to you if you’d like to only bake it until melted or take it one step further by letting your gnocchi sit under the broiler for a minute to get some attractive browned spots. Whichever you choose, we definitely recommend the final basil garnish to add flavor and freshness to your final dish.

Storage:Have leftovers? Store them in an airtight container in the fridge for 3-4 days.

#6593. Katy Perry and Justin Trudeau Have a Rare Red Carpet Date Night

The couple dressed up for Baby2Baby’s annual gala.

Katy Perry and Justin Trudeau have another red-carpet appearance to add to their relationship timeline. On Saturday, November 14, the singer and former Canadian prime minister stepped out together for the 2026 Baby2Baby Gala presented by Paul Mitchell at the Pacific Design Center in West Hollywood, California.

The couple smiled and posed together affectionately in complementary ensembles.

The outing was in support of Baby2Baby, a nonprofit organization that provides essential items to children living in poverty across the U.S.. Its annual gala raises millions of dollars to fund that work, bringing together celebrities, philanthropists, and business leaders. Helmed by co-CEOs Kelly Sawyer Patricof and Norah Weinstein, this year’s celebrity attendees included Cardi B, Barbara Palvin, Dylan Sprouse, Ciara, Jessica Alba, and Kerry Washington.

This year’s event honored Demi Moore with the Giving Tree Award, recognizing her commitment to children in need. Previous honorees include Serena Williams and Charlize Theron.

For the evening, Perry wore a look from Antonio Grimaldi’s spring 2025 couture collection, pairing a strapless metallic minidress with a floor-length champagne-colored skirt. Trudeau coordinated with her in soft hues, wearing a cream tuxedo jacket, white dress shirt, black bow tie, and black trousers.

The evening marked their third red carpet appearance together, following their debut at the Tribeca Festival in June and their more recent appearance at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s opening in September.

#6592. Alexander Skarsgård Pairs Mint Green With Bubblegum Pink for a Colorful JW Anderson Fit

Whether he’s wearing fashion’s favorite kilt or pairing a gold suit with transparent Oxford shoes, Alexander Skarsgård always delivers on the red carpet. And his latest look was no exception.

Yesterday, the Swedish actor showed up to the Directors Guild of America (DGA) theater for the all-day Deadline Contenders Film event—an awards-season program that spotlighted the cast and crew of 15 major films from the past year. Skarsgård was there to promote his most recent project, Wicker, sitting down for a panel discussion with co-writers and co-directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston, and prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley. And while his fellow creatives kept things simple with jeans and neutral palettes, he stood out in a bright, colorful ensemble.

On top, the look featured a mint-green JW Anderson rugby shirt, designed with a white collar and elongated placket. The cozy oversize polo was embroidered with the word “Baby” in satin, in a font inspired by pieces of text found in vintage magazines.

Skarsgård’s hot-pink shorts, from the same label, were crafted in collaboration with Humphries Weaving. Founded in 1972 in Sudbury, England, the company has become known for its bespoke silk fabrics, which are woven using historically-accurate techniques and often adorn the interiors of stately and royal residences. Here, in partnership with creative director Jonathan Anderson, Humphries developed a 100% silk damask with dotted-line motifs.

The True Blood actor finished things off with black socks and matching loafers.

Wicker, in which Skarsgård played a man literally made of wicker, made its theatrical release last month.

Luckily, we've done the rummaging for you, turning up a GQ-endorsed assortment of gifts that look like you put in considerably more effort than a few clicks and two-day shipping.

Still searching? Browse the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas that are actually worth giving.

A teeny-tiny digital camera on a keychain, packaged in a blind box. Half the fun is seeing which retro design you get.

A remote control for turning pages on your Kindle. We have peaked as a society.

The Kodak Pixpro has emerged as a go-to budget option for anyone looking to embrace the point-and-shoot life.

Timex's classic Ironman Triathlon is a no-nonsense sports ticker with everything you need and nothing you don't.

Tinned fish is an elite stocking stuffer. Especially when it's packaged as beautifully as Fishwife does it.

The iconic Hanes Beefy-T turned 50 this year, and it's still the undisputed heavyweight champion of any dude's T-shirt drawer.

Our pick for the best underwear to buy in bulk, Calvin Klein's stretch briefs are as classic as they get. An easy gift they'll actually use.

The only thing better than a Dickies Eisenhower is a warmer Dickies Eisenhower. This lined version retains everything that makes the original a legend while offering a little extra protection against the cold.

Cashmere is one of life's great pleasures, and Naadam makes it possible to indulge without going broke.

A bomber jacket built to military spec by the brand that made it famous. 'Nuff said, really.

You could get them a fancier hoodie, but there's nothing wrong with sticking to the classics. Russell is an OG in the game, and its Dri-Power fleece hoodie is practically return-proof.

Ralph gave us the gift of the Polo Bear. Now you can give the gift of the Polo Bear on a terrific beanie.

Dress socks are one of the easiest wardrobe upgrades—and these Polo Ralph Lauren crews are cushy, classic, and primed for all the holiday shindigs filling up your calendar.

Fact: A guy can always use another polo shirt. Lacoste's iconic cotton-piqué original has the perfect combination of heft and breathability, not to mention nearly a century of good taste behind it.

Time and again, the Levi's 501 ends up right back at the top of our jeans guide. Some things never go out of style, and a great pair of straight-leg jeans is one of them.

Reebok's Club C Vintage has long been a favorite around GQ, and it might just be the best sneaker the Everything Store has to offer.

The 997H is the more affordable, everyday-minded cousin of New Balance's premium 997, with much of the same dad-shoe charm at a fraction of the price.

From Brooklyn to Berlin to just about anywhere else with a winter, the Carhartt watch cap is practically standard issue. And at this price, you can afford to outfit the whole crew.

Merrell's Moab 3 is a tried-and-true hiking boot, and gifting a pair might be just the nudge they need to get off the couch and onto a trail.

There's no shortage of loafers out there, but Sebago makes a particularly good one.

A burly rugby from Taylor Stitch might be just what their wardrobe needs. And its clean look means pretty much anyone can rock it.

Who gifts a whole damn bar cart? From Amazon, no less? Well, Umbra makes a great one, and you don't have to tell them where you got it.

Gift them a wall sconce that doesn't require an electrician or a security deposit sacrifice. Renter-friendly lighting has rarely looked this good.

Ozlo's souped-up Sleepbuds are built for the serious business of getting some shut-eye, with noise-masking sounds, a built-in alarm, and a fit comfortable enough to sleep in.

#6590. Thanksgiving Jungle Juice

While I love individual Thanksgiving cocktails, if you're serving a big crowd, a punch like this one is the way to go. If you need to save your energy for cooking and serving up the food this turkey day, then whip up this shareable Thanksgiving jungle juice, and let your guests serve themselves all day long. Made with two bottles of red wine, whiskey, and Fireball, this punch is the drink to serve if you're looking to party this holiday.

#6588. Ayo Edebiri Got the Forehead Curl Memo

Ayo Edebiri is one of the best-dressed people in Hollywood. In 2024, GQ named her a rising star in menswear. At our 2026 Men of the Year party, she made an even stronger case for herself as a style icon for the ages. Walking the red carpet at the Chateau Marmont in West Hollywood, the Emmy-winning actor continued her winning streak of power suiting in a navy chalk-stripe ensemble, a bright emerald-turquoise dress shirt, and a burgundy geometric tie. Her bob was styled in a side part, with a pronounced curl sweeping across her forehead. It’s a look that’s become a staple among Hollywood’s best-dressed men this year, a callback to Superman’s signature swoop, minus the Spandex tights and cape.

In the 1920s, the playful wisp of hair was known as the kiss curl: a deliberately placed lock of hair that sat on the forehead, even amid an otherwise carefully sculpted ’do. (As Seth Rogen helpfully pointed out on Instagram after we noted the kiss curl’s 2026 resurgence: “It’s called a Forelock.”) Its prominence in men’s grooming can be traced back in part to the French-American entertainer Josephine Baker, whose iconic curl ushered in an era—and now a century—of rogue forehead curls.

The kiss curl was so emblematic of the era that it made a triumphant return at the 2025 Met Gala, themed “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.” A host of women paired the look with impeccable tailoring, including Simone Biles, Taraji P. Henson, Teyana Taylor, and, yes, Ayo Edebiri.

The modern appeal of the forehead curl is easy to understand. As hairstyles have grown longer, looser, and less structured, the curl lends an air of studied nonchalance—as if you didn’t spend too much time getting your hair just right. It’s sexy in a just-got-out-of-bed kind of way, especially when everything else—from the rest of the hair to the outfit—remains crisp, clean, and pristine.

As Edebiri once told Vogue of dressing for the red carpet: “One of the fun parts of getting to do this sort of thing is that you get to transform and be these different permutations of yourself.” At GQ’s Men of the Year party, she once again understood the assignment.

From Emma Stone to Zendaya and Charlize Theron

The Governors Awards are back. The annual gala hosted by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (who also hosts the Oscars) to honor lifetime achievement and extraordinary contributions to film has returned for its 17th edition—and the red carpet is brimming with star power.

While this gala itself is not aired live, like the main Oscars ceremony (which takes place in March every year), the awards given are considered genuine Oscars. But there were plenty of other guests in attendance this evening at the Ray Dolby Ballroom at Ovation Hollywood in Los Angeles—from Penélope Cruz in Chanel to Zendaya in Gilles Deacon, Charlize Theron in Tom Ford, Tessa Thompson in Schiaparelli, and Emma Stone in Louis Vuitton.

#6584. Cream Cheese Mashed Potatoes

Cream cheese doesn't just belong on bagels. In this instance, it's the secret to making mashed potatoes even creamier, richer, and more decadent. The high fat content in the cream cheese melds with the butter and milk to make the potatoes perfectly fluffy and creamy. Serve these at your Thanksgiving or Christmas dinner, or even on a cozy weeknight alongside oven-baked pork chops.

What People Are Saying:“Never cooked mashed potatoes before, and this recipe turned out amazing.” - GreenHat

“Silky smooth and delicious” - BlueProcessor

In a large pot, cover the potatoes with water and season with salt. Bring it to a boil and cook until the potatoes are softened and fork-tender, which should take about 16 to 18 minutes. Drain and return the potatoes to the pot.

Add cream cheese and, using a potato masher, mash potatoes until smooth.

Meanwhile, in a small saucepan over medium heat, cook the milk and butter. Stir until the butter is melted, which should take about 2 minutes. Pour the butter mixture over the potatoes.

Stir until it's combined and creamy. Make sure to season with salt and pepper!

Transfer potatoes to a serving bowl and season with more pepper. Top with chives and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store leftover cream cheese mashed potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.
